items.title: CAN 2027, l’Algérie domine la Zambie : Hemdani réussit son premier test
items.description: Avec une équipe largement remaniée par rapport à celle qui a disputé le Mondial 2026, l’Algérie a dominé la Zambie (3-1) et Brahim Hemdani a réussi son premier test lors de la première journée des éliminatoires de la CAN 2027, ce vendredi 25 septembre au stade Hocine Ait Ahmed de Tizi-Ouzou. Les Fennecs n’ont pas attendu longtemps pour montrer leurs griffes. Dès la 2 e minute, Ibrahim Maza , en véritable meneur de jeu, récupère le ballon et sert Mohamed Amoura. Algérie – Zambie : les Fennecs commencent bien L’attaquant de l’OGC Nice n’attend pas et glisse le ballon à Jaouen Hadjam qui tire dans l’angle fermé pour ouvrir le score (1-0, 2 e ). Un but inscrit grâce à une contre-attaque rapidement menée et un travail collectif à une touche de balle. Ce but donne des ailes aux Fennecs qui assiègent le camp zambien et étouffent leurs adversaires, inexistants en première période. En grande forme en ce début de saison avec son club Hull City en Premier League, Mohamed Belloumi s’est montré particulièrement entreprenant, réussissant à se créer des occasions, sans aller jusqu’au bout. À la 18 e minute, Amine Gouiri se blesse et laisse sa place à Amin Chiakha. La première mi-temps se termine sur un léger avantage pour les hommes de Brahim Hemdani. En seconde période, même scénario, avec une large domination des Fennecs. Mohamed Amoura rate le break à la 54 e minute de jeu, après une passe lumineuse de Maza, encore lui. Le tir de l’attaquant de Nice passe à côté du poteau du gardien zambien. Quatre minutes après, c’est la Zambie qui profite du manque d’efficacité des Verts et de la passivité de la défense algérienne pour égaliser. Sakala se balade sur le coté gauche et son tir trouve le petit filet de Melvin Mastil (1-1, 58 e ). Algérie – Zambie : Hemdani commence avec une victoire Sans se décourager, les camarades de Ramy Bensebaini repartent à l’assaut du gardien adverse pour reprendre l’avantage et c’est Ibrahim Maza, excellent depuis le début de la rencontre, qui, bien servi par Amoura, réussit à tromper d’un tir croisé le gardien Mwanza, coupable d’une erreur sur ce but (67 e , 2-1). L’Algérie reprend l’avantage. Le même Maza sert ensuite Hadj Moussa pour faire le break (3-1, 74 e ) et sceller la première victoire des Fennecs de l’ère Hemdani. Le nouveau coach des Verts entame sa mission avec une belle victoire obtenue par une équipe jeune et talentueuse. L’Algérie doit confirmer son bon début dans les éliminatoires de la CAN 2027 face au Burundi le 29 septembre prochain à Bujumbura. L’article CAN 2027, l’Algérie domine la Zambie : Hemdani réussit son premier test est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: Le ministère des mines réduit à 200 km2 les superficies accordées pour les permis de prospections minières
items.description: Le ministère mauritanien des Mines et de l'Industrie a fixé un nouveau plafond pour la superficie des permis de prospection minière, de sorte que la superficie d'un même permis ne dépasse pas 200 kilomètres carrés pour les minéraux des groupes de 1 à 6. Le ministère a indiqué, dans des directives publiées ce vendredi par le ministre Eddi Ould Zeine, que ces mesures visaient à réguler et à encadrer les superficies accordées pour la prospection minière, afin de garantir la rationalisation et la durabilité des investissements dans le secteur minier national, tout en respectant les plafonds légaux fixés par le Code minier modifié et renforcé par les lois applicables. Il a ajouté que les demandes enregistrées auprès de la Direction du registre minier dont la superficie dépasse 200 kilomètres carrés feront l’objet d’une réduction en concertation avec leurs titulaires, avant l’émission de l’avis de paiement, précisant que ces mesures s’appliqueront immédiatement à toutes les demandes de prospection enregistrées. Le ministère a précisé que ces directives visent à encourager les acteurs et les investisseurs à mener des efforts d’exploration sur le terrain adaptés à leurs capacités techniques et financières, et à empêcher le monopole de vastes superficies sans exploitation effective, afin de garantir une répartition équitable et équilibrée des superficies disponibles.

items.title: Vice President calls for stronger local pharmaceutical production to reduce medicine imports
items.description: Vice President Professor Naana Jane Opoku-Agyemang has called for stronger local pharmaceutical production as Ghana seeks to reduce its reliance on imported medicines and improve access to essential drugs. She said expanding the capacity of Ghanaian pharmaceutical manufacturers would strengthen the health system and help the country respond more effectively to changing healthcare needs. The Vice President was speaking in Accra at the opening of the 90th Anniversary Annual General Meeting and Scientific Conference of the Pharmaceutical Society of Ghana. She noted that local manufacturers were already building capacity to produce a wider range of essential medicines and pharmaceutical products. “Local manufacturers are developing capacity to produce infusions, injectables, ophthalmic products and anaesthetics,” she said. Professor Opoku-Agyemang said increasing local production would not only strengthen the pharmaceutical industry but also improve access to essential medicines. The government is pursuing a five-year strategy to increase the proportion of medicines manufactured locally from 30% to 70%. Pharmaceutical Society calls for funding President of the Pharmaceutical Society of Ghana, Pharm. Paul Owusu Donkor, welcomed the 70% target but said achieving it would require sustained government support. “We therefore ask the government of Ghana to turn its five-year strategy into a funded delivery program,” he said. He called for predictable public procurement of quality-assured medicines manufactured in Ghana, timely payment of suppliers and access to affordable long-term financing for pharmaceutical manufacturers. According to him, these measures would give local producers greater certainty to invest in production capacity and contribute to the government’s target. Focus on changing health needs Beyond pharmaceutical manufacturing, Professor Opoku-Agyemang urged pharmacists to play a greater role in addressing Ghana’s growing burden of chronic and non-communicable diseases. She also called for regulation to keep pace with technological changes affecting healthcare, including artificial intelligence, digital prescribing and evolving medicine supply chains. The Vice President said Ghana’s changing health needs require a health system capable of detecting diseases early, managing conditions effectively and preventing avoidable complications. The conference is being held under the theme “Science. Impact. Legacy: 90 Years of Pharmaceutical Excellence.” The 90th anniversary event is providing a platform for discussions on the future of Ghana’s pharmaceutical sector, access to medicines and measures to build greater resilience within the health system.

items.title: 2027: ‘Atiku’s victory will end rotational presidency’ — Shehu Sani
items.description: Former Kaduna Central Senator, Shehu Sani, has warned that the informal arrangement of rotating the presidency between Nigeria’s northern and southern regions could come to an end if African Democratic Congress (ADC) candidate Atiku Abubakar wins the 2027 election. Sani made the comment on Channels Television’s Politics Today on Friday while arguing that political parties should field southern candidates in the 2027 presidential election. “If Atiku wins, it means that is the end of rotational presidency in Nigeria, and there is going to be hard and bitter feelings from the southern part of Nigeria. I don’t think anyone will like to preside over a country full of hate, animosity, and conflict. Right now, the political system is managing a lot of crises,” he said. “I don’t think a northerner taking over power here will come in with ease and conveniently to the people in the southern part of Nigeria. But if we allow the South to have their eight years, by 2031, a northerner takes over, there will be no challenge from southern Nigeria. That is my own view.” Sani, however, acknowledged that the Constitution does not prevent Atiku or any other northerner from contesting the presidency. “I never said Atiku should not run. Constitutionally, he has a right to run for any election, but what I said was that a southern part of Nigeria should be allowed to have its eight-year tenure in office, just like the way the North has from 2015 to 2023,” he said. He called on opposition parties to field southern candidates and allow the region to compete for the presidency in 2027. “The NDC should field Peter Obi, the APM should field Makinde, let the South struggle it out and see who wins for four years. And when the tenure is done by 2031, the North should have its unchallengeable opportunity to produce the leadership of the country,” Sani said. He also rejected the argument that a region’s larger population or electorate should automatically translate into prolonged control of the presidency. “You cannot say that because you have the largest electorate and population, so you should continue dominating politics,” he said. The post 2027: ‘Atiku’s victory will end rotational presidency’ — Shehu Sani appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Partenariat tuniso-suisse pour la digitalisation de l’administration du travail
items.description: La Coopération suisse en Tunisie a soutenu le lancement d'une nouvelle plateforme numérique dédiée à l'administration du travail, portée par le Ministère des Affaires Sociales avec l'appui du Bureau de l’OIT à Alger pour les pays du Maghreb. ​Fruit de plusieurs mois de travail avec les équipes du Ministère, cet outil permettra de mieux exploiter les données, renforcer le suivi de l'action des inspecteurs du travail et faciliter l'accès à l'information au quotidien, indique l'ambassade Suisse, qui réaffirme son accompagnement de la Tunisie à la digitalisation de l'administration du travail Ce lancement marque également le début d'une nouvelle phase : celle de l'appropriation de cet outil par les équipes sur le terrain, lit-on encore dans le communiqué, qui précise que cette initiative est menée dans le cadre du projet « Un dialogue social responsable et inclusif pour une cohésion sociale pérenne en Tunisie », avec l'appui du Fonds des Nations Unies pour la consolidation de la paix (PBF) et de la Direction du développement et de la coopération. Y. N. L’article Partenariat tuniso-suisse pour la digitalisation de l'administration du travail est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.description: L'équipe nationale masculine mauritanienne s'est imposée 3-1 face à l'équipe de Jersey, tandis que le joueur Abdallah Khaled a obtenu le titre de candidat maître international (CM) lors des Olympiades d'échecs de Samarcande, selon la Fédération mauritanienne des échecs. La fédération a ajouté que Fatima Cheikh Sidiya et Bouchra Aba ont obtenu le titre de candidate maître international féminin (WCM), portant ainsi à six le nombre de titres internationaux remportés par les joueurs mauritaniens lors de ce tournoi. Ces trois nouveaux titres s’ajoutent à ceux remportés hier par Mokhtar Sidati, Ahmed Cherif Khaled et Fatima El-Haj Sidi. La fédération a déclaré que ces six titres représentaient le meilleur résultat jamais obtenu par la Mauritanie lors d’un seul tournoi, sans toutefois fournir de détails sur les critères sur lesquels elle s’est appuyée pour qualifier ce résultat de record.

items.title: The brewing tension at KNUST; Beware the Ides of October….
items.description: Less than a month after the investiture of a new Vice-Chancellor, the Governing Council of KNUST has decided to end a practice that has been part of KNUST’s academic governance for generations: faculty will no longer elect their own Deans and Pro-Vice-Chancellors. They will be appointed. The timing alone should make everyone pause. A new administration has barely settled in, and already one of the University’s longest-standing traditions of academic participation is being dismantled. Even more troubling is that Council is proceeding despite formal petitions from the major recognized staff unions, UTAG, GAUA and TEWU-TUC, strongly opposing the change. These are not peripheral voices; they represent the staff whose participation in the governance of the University is now being removed. It is therefore much bigger than a change in procedure; it is a transfer of power from the academic community to the centre. From time immemorial, academics and senior administrators have had a say in choosing their academic leaders. The system may have had weaknesses, but it has also produced leaders who enjoyed the confidence of the academic community (Professors Rita Dickson, Otoo Ellis, Adarkwa, and Odai are examples). If there are problems with the elections, fix them, tighten the rules, and improve the safeguards while making the process more transparent. But don’t abolish participation because it is difficult to manage. There is also a democratic irony that should not be lost on us. In Ghana today, ‘even’ a head porter has the constitutional right to participate in choosing the President of the Republic. Yet at KNUST, academics and senior administrators (the people who teach, research, supervise students and run the academic enterprise) are being denied the opportunity to participate in choosing those who lead their academic units. Today it is Deans and ProVCs; tomorrow, what other forms of participation might be considered unnecessary or inconvenient? October 2018 should still be fresh in our minds; a disagreement at KNUST escalated into a major institutional crisis, leading to disruption, destruction of property, closure of the University and dissolution of the Governing Council. We should be doing everything possible to ensure that history does not repeat itself. Council has the authority to make decisions, yes. But having the authority to do something does not necessarily make every decision you take right. Good governance is not simply about the power to decide; it is also about knowing when to listen, when to consult, and when to reconsider. And let us be clear: this is not merely about who becomes Dean or ProVC; it is about what kind of KNUST we want. A University that teaches critical thinking cannot afford to become intolerant of critical voices within its own walls. KNUST has only recently restored its academic calendar after considerable disruption. The last thing the University needs is another avoidable confrontation. If this dispute escalates, students, lecturers, researchers and ultimately the University’s reputation will suffer. We have been here before. KNUST does not need another October 2018. It needs dialogue, consultation and statesmanship now. Council should pause and engage the unions seriously. Because once you take away a community’s voice, you cannot simply expect its trust to remain intact.

items.title: Egypt’s Warning to Israel
items.description: W hen Israel’s leaders gathered in Jerusalem on September 26, 2023, to mark the 50th anniversary of the Yom Kippur War, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu described the surprise assault by Syria and Egypt as a cautionary tale, one of missed intelligence warnings and self-delusion. “We do not underestimate any threat,” he said. Roughly two hours before Netanyahu took the stage, a chartered Cessna jet linked to Egypt’s intelligence service had touched down at Ben Gurion Airport, about 30 miles away. The jet rolled to a stop in an isolated section of the airport used for sensitive diplomatic and security missions. Abbas Kamel, Egypt’s intelligence chief and one of the region’s most influential security officials, had come to Israel on a most sensitive mission. Hamas, the Muslim Brotherhood–aligned terrorist group that controlled Gaza, appeared to be mobilizing for a major attack, Kamel said, according to Israeli, Egyptian, Arab, U.S., and European officials who were briefed about his visit after October 7. The window to prevent a disaster was closing. He recommended that the Israeli government grant Hamas economic concessions to avert conflict. His message, according to one former Israeli official later briefed on the visit, was: If you don’t change course, Gaza is going to blow up in your faces. Kamel didn’t provide Israeli officials with a date or specific information on what turned out to be a multipronged attack on Israel less than two weeks later, on October 7. And it’s not clear exactly with whom he met. The Egyptian plane remained on the ground in Israel for 67 minutes, according to an Israeli-airport-authority flight log, before returning to Cairo. (Independent flight-tracking applications confirm the plane’s journey.) What the Israeli officials did with Kamel’s warning remains an open question three years after the most devastating surprise attack in Israel’s history. But officials from seven different countries I spoke with said that Kamel’s visit should have set off alarms across the top ranks of the Israeli government. Netanyahu attended a classified briefing following the Yom Kippur War commemoration, according to his public schedule, and soon after approved some economic concessions to Hamas. Officials who spoke with me stressed that the mere presence of the Egyptian intelligence chief in Israel should have demonstrated the urgency of the issue. “The messenger was the message,” a former Israeli official told me. “There is no world,” this official said, where top Israeli officials meet with the head of Egyptian intelligence “and Bibi is not aware.” Netanyahu’s office, in the days after the attack, denied that he’d received any warnings, directly or indirectly, from Egypt over the situation in Gaza. Spokesmen for Netanyahu and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi didn’t respond to my repeated requests for comment when I asked about Kamel’s visit. The then-head of Netanyahu’s national-security council, Tzachi Hanegbi, denied to me this week that there had been a visit from Kamel or an Egyptian warning of any kind. Kamel’s 2023 visit, details of which have not been previously reported, underscores what dozens of sources have told me: that the Israeli government was repeatedly told of threatening activity by Hamas in the lead-up to October 7. A United Nations envoy who was in the Middle East at the time publicly warned of a latent conflict that could bring “grave consequences” while privately scrambling to defuse tensions between Israel and Hamas. The president of the United Arab Emirates, Mohamed bin Zayed, called Netanyahu to warn about the possibility of an imminent attack, after being briefed on intelligence findings from Egyptian and Palestinian sources, according to U.S. and Arab officials with knowledge of the call. Earlier this month, Israel’s Haaretz reported the leaders’ call; I confirmed with multiple officials that the call took place. Netanyahu denied the report and has threatened to sue Haaretz . The UAE didn’t respond to a request for comment. [ Read: Netanyahu just admitted he’s unfit to lead Israel ] Current and former Israeli, Arab, and U.S. officials in Israel tell me that they all experienced the same phenomenon in 2023: an arrogance on the part of Netanyahu bred by the deep-seated belief that Israel had the upper hand against Hamas. “It seemed clear that, for whatever reason, the West Bank was their priority,” a former senior U.S. official involved in talks with the Israeli government told me. “They were confident—even cocky—that they had the situation under control.” The Hamas attack, 11 days after Kamel’s visit, resulted in the deaths of approximately 1,200 people, primarily civilians, and the abduction into Gaza of 251 hostages during coordinated raids on communities, military bases, and an outdoor music festival. Israel launched a crushing retaliatory campaign that killed more than 73,000 Palestinians in Gaza, the majority of whom were civilians, according to the territory’s Health Ministry. Hamas’s leadership and thousands of combatants have been killed. The attacks on Israel and the Gaza war that followed produced one of the more devastating humanitarian tragedies of the 21st century. The Netanyahu government’s stunning lack of preparation before the October 7 invasion is perhaps the most important issue in next month’s Israeli election. Netanyahu, who has been prime minister longer than any other politician in Israel’s history, is facing the most serious challenge of his career. Many Israelis, including Netanyahu’s main rival, the former military chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot, have demanded an independent state inquiry into the military and intelligence failures in the run-up to the October 7 attacks. But Netanyahu has continuously refused to set up the kind of independent inquiry that followed past security failures, including the Yom Kippur War. The prime minister has instead attempted to establish a politically appointed commission of inquiry, which he said would include opposition representatives. The attempt was highly controversial; opposition leaders have refused to advance the proposal over concerns that the probe would favor Netanyahu’s government. While the wait for an inquiry continues, dozens of current and former Israeli, Egyptian, Arab, European, and U.S. officials have spoken with me, and their accounts help tell the story of what went wrong that fall. S ince Egypt and Israel signed the Camp David peace accords, in 1978, their relationship can be described as, at best, a cold peace. But the two nations have a common desire to subdue the threat of Hamas and other militant groups in Gaza, which borders both countries. Intelligence sharing between Egypt and Israel has thrived, particularly since al-Sisi became president, in 2014—even when their diplomatic relationship founders. Most of the intelligence reports in the weeks before the October 7 attacks, including Egypt’s, pointed to the renewal of conventional attacks—such as rocket fire—by Hamas and other armed factions in Gaza. They also warned of a spillover of violence into the West Bank. But intelligence sources inside Gaza conveyed to Egypt a more ominous picture, leading Egypt and the UAE to flag to Israel the prospect that something unprecedented was in the works. “For Kamel to go to Israel” for a single hour, an Egyptian official told me about the September 2023 visit, “meant that al-Sisi himself felt: You need to go there and tell them yourself .” The Israeli government’s focus, however, was elsewhere. The country was already in the grip of its deepest domestic crisis in decades. For months, Israel had been consumed by Netanyahu’s effort to overhaul the judicial system, a constitutional confrontation that was protested by hundreds of thousands and opened deep fissures within the military and within society. And a surge in Israeli-Palestinian violence in the West Bank had already made 2023 the deadliest year in decades for West Bank Palestinians, with Israeli military raids, Palestinian attacks, and settler violence contributing to the combustible atmosphere. Israel surged military personnel and resources into the territory. Biden administration officials sought to ease tensions in the West Bank while other international and regional negotiators focused on Gaza. [ Read: Israel can’t postpone its reckoning forever ] Israel established a comprehensive land, sea, and air blockade of Gaza in 2007, when Hamas seized control of the territory, and crossings at Egypt’s border with Gaza, in Rafah, have been tightly restricted since. Freedom of movement became virtually impossible for the 2.1 million people who lived in the 141-square-mile territory. Israel and Hamas had last fought a war there in May 2021. That 11-day conflict ended in a cease-fire—brokered, notably, by Kamel, among others. Hamas appeared to have little interest in abandoning the uneasy truce. But international observers picked up on signs that the situation inside Gaza was changing. Long before the summer of 2023, one international negotiator in the region told me, contacts were reporting that “something was cooking,” though the details were vague and the signals confusing. By August, tensions in Gaza had clearly heightened, in part because Qatar froze deliveries of Egyptian fuel that it had been sending to Gaza since 2021. Hamas resold the fuel and used the proceeds to help pay public-sector workers, a key mechanism by which it maintained control in the Strip. Hamas called for demonstrations at the Erez border crossing over Qatar’s delayed aid, as well as other lingering disputes like the treatment of Palestinian prisoners. The crossing is the primary pedestrian gateway between Israel and Gaza and an especially important one for Gazan workers. Israel responded to the protests in mid-September by closing the crossing. Roughly 18,000 Gazans had permits to work in Israel. After those people were barred from going to work, “the escalation started to come much faster,” one negotiator told me. The Arabic outlet Rai al-Youm , citing Palestinian sources, reported on September 26 that Hamas had conveyed to the Egyptian government that Gaza would explode over the Erez closure. That same day, Kamel’s plane flew to Israel. Negotiators from Egypt, Qatar, and the United Nations scrambled to maintain calm. Hamas officials responded with what one international negotiator described as a broad “shopping list” of demands, including more permits to work inside Israel and the restoration of the fuel-for-public-salaries arrangement with Qatar. After the talks concluded in the final days of September, Hamas agreed to pull people back from the border fence and to try to ease tensions. Israel agreed to reopen the Erez crossing and to restore a medical-supply line into Gaza, adding that it would consider increasing the number of work permits. Still, the situation remained turbulent. On September 27, 10 days before the attack, Tor Wennesland, the UN’s special coordinator for the Middle East peace process, left Gaza with a stark warning: “The situation inside the Strip is dire and we must avoid another conflict that will have grave consequences for all,” Wennesland wrote on X. A day later, the new arrangement appeared to be taking hold. European diplomats who visited Erez watched as Gazan workers streamed back into Israel. But negotiators told me it later became clear that Hamas was using the talks as a ploy to buy time while finalizing its attack plans. Documents recovered by Israel from Gaza revealed that Hamas regarded the 2021 conflict as a triumph, and in its aftermath began planning for a breathtakingly large operation. A detailed memorandum from August 2022, apparently handwritten by Yahya Sinwar, then the leader of Hamas in Gaza, laid out much of the operational plan that the group would put into effect the following year. Even as international mediators focused on issues such as work permits and fuel deliveries, believing that these could defuse tensions, Hamas continued its relentless preparations for a massive attack. U.S. and Israeli military analysts told me Israel misinterpreted Hamas’s intentions, concluding that the group had no desire for military confrontation. K amel’s visits to Israel are rare. His last known trips were in May and August 2021, following that year’s Israel-Hamas war. After Kamel’s September 2023 trip, Egypt continued to raise the alarm up until two days before the attack, according to U.S., Egyptian, and Israeli officials with direct knowledge of those communications. American and Israeli officials told me it is unclear whether Kamel’s message could have been understood as foretelling the unprecedented attack that followed. Most of the warnings that Israel received in 2023 contained no date, target, or method of attack. But they were frequent and persistent. Around the same time, Netanyahu received the call from bin Zayed, whose country had normalized relations with Israel only three years earlier. In the call, bin Zayed reportedly sought to convey his assessment that Sinwar was planning a major attack. Like Kamel, bin Zayed urged Netanyahu to make economic concessions to Gaza. But Netanyahu seemed unmoved, two Arab officials familiar with the call told me. UN negotiators, U.S. officials, and international groups sensed that tensions in Gaza were exceptionally high, but told me they hadn’t been aware of any particular plans for an attack. On September 28, the CIA issued an internal report about a possible Hamas escalation in Gaza, reportedly based in part on foreign intelligence services. U.S. officials told me that report described the possibility that Hamas would launch rockets into Israel over several days. A second report, dated October 5, built on the first but was more analytical than revelatory. Neither detected rehearsals for a coordinated, multipronged attack like the one Hamas carried out two days later. On October 5, a message from Egypt to Israel also reiterated concerns that the situation was untenable, U.S., Egyptian and Israeli officials said. It provided no date or methodology, but conveyed urgency about a possible attack, the officials said. Egypt also shared its assessments with several other nations in the region, including Saudi Arabia, a senior Gulf Arab official told me. Jordan’s intelligence chief also conveyed concerns to his Israeli counterparts, according to Arab officials, that the situation had grown potentially explosive, especially in the West Bank, and needed to be addressed swiftly. (Spokespeople for Jordan’s government and intelligence service didn’t respond to a request for comment.) Biden-administration officials told me that neither Egypt nor the UAE shared such warnings with them ahead of October 7. U.S., Egyptian, Arab, and Israeli officials gave me a range of reasons why. Several people told me the warnings were too vague to warrant sharing with the U.S. Other officials, including those from the region, told me it was up to Netanyahu’s government to share the findings with Washington. (U.S. officials I spoke with dismissed this explanation, suggesting that if Egypt or Abu Dhabi had a pressing warning for Israel, Washington should have heard about it from them.) Several months after the attack, CIA Director William Burns was told, almost in passing, about both Kamel’s visit to Israel and bin Zayed’s call, but was not told about the specifics of their outreach, according to U.S., Israeli, and Arab officials. [ Read: Netanyahu doesn’t want the truth to come out ] Two days after the attack, as Israel took stock of the tragedy and its military campaign in Gaza began, Netanyahu’s office rejected press reports that he’d received any outreach from Kamel or Egypt. “The Prime Minister has neither spoken, nor met, with the head of Egyptian intelligence since the formation of the government, neither directly nor indirectly,” his office said on X . But the distinction between direct contact and intelligence passed through aides and other officials would become central to the debate over whether Israel could have done more to anticipate the attacks. On October 11, then–House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Michael McCaul told reporters after a classified briefing for lawmakers that Egypt had warned Israel. “We know that Egypt had warned the Israelis three days prior that an event like this could happen,” McCaul said. “I don’t want to get too much into classified, but a warning was given. I think the question was at what level.” (McCaul didn’t respond to my repeated attempts to discuss his comments.) In the months that followed, Israeli officials described a broader failure to interpret the signals coming from Gaza. In leaked recordings of briefings to bereaved families and residents obtained by Israel’s Channel 12, Herzi Halevi, then the chief of staff of the Israel Defense Forces, described the military establishment as having been “ lulled to sleep .” In a separate leaked recording , Halevi told local council chiefs that before the attacks, he had regarded Gaza “as the last border that needed attention.” Halevi resigned from his position in March 2025, and that June, the head of the Israel Security Agency, Ronen Bar, resigned under pressure over intelligence failures linked to the October 7 attacks. Hanegbi, the head of Netanyahu’s security council, was replaced in October 2025. Kamel, who left Egypt’s General Intelligence Service in October 2024, is now an adviser and special envoy for al-Sisi. S ince the October 7 attacks , Israel not only launched a crushing retaliation in Gaza, but later opened military fronts against Lebanon’s Hezbollah and, this year, a war in Iran. It’s impossible to know what would have happened if the warnings from Kamel and others had been heeded at the time, but it’s hard to imagine that Israel wouldn’t have been better prepared. As it was, the attacks caught the Israeli security services flat-footed. Reserve forces weren’t immediately available after kibbutz communities were attacked, leaving them defended primarily by local, lightly armed civilian volunteer forces from about 6:30 a.m., when the attacks began, to 1:30 p.m., when significant IDF reinforcements arrived. Netanyahu said in a campaign video clip last month that Israeli security officials failed to immediately wake him on the morning of October 7. “In the lead-up to October, there were so many warning signs, so many indications, that an attack was imminent,” Netanyahu said, without offering any specifics. “Had they woken me up, everything would have looked different. That is the story of October 7th—that is the story.” Today, Gaza remains in ruins and violence continues, despite efforts by the Biden and Trump administrations to secure a cease-fire. An April assessment by the UN, the World Bank, and the European Union estimated that $71.4 billion would be needed over the next decade for Gaza’s recovery and reconstruction. The great majority of its population remains displaced. Meanwhile, the trauma of October 7 lives on for Israelis. And bereaved families from that day continue to search for answers about how Hamas was able to engage in a devastating attack on Israel that appeared to catch the government completely by surprise. Jack Rodriquez-Vars contributed reporting to this story * Illustration sources: Getty; Khaled Desouki / AFP / Getty; Anadolu / Getty; Fatih Aktas / Anadolu / Getty

items.title: Primetime Wrings Even More Drama Out of To Catch a Predator
items.description: To Catch a Predator may have presented a simulation of reality, but it was just convincing enough for viewers. The show’s objective was to apprehend people suspected of child sex abuse—which it did by staging sting operations. Its host, Chris Hansen, and his collaborators at Dateline NBC would sparsely furnish the entryway of some rented suburban home; an adult actor posing as a teenager would open the door for a stranger he or she had been chatting with online; and Hansen, who worked as a Dateline correspondent, would lurk in another room, waiting for the right moment to present himself to the houseguest and laconically intervene. His catchphrase was “Have a seat,” which he would utter while inviting his latest subject to take stock of the nightmare unfolding around him: He was suspected of intending to have sex with a minor, Hansen would explain, and now they were on candid camera—the police waiting just outside. Hansen’s somewhat maniacal pursuit of what he considered justice was detailed in last year’s very solid documentary Predators , which explored the legal and ethical limits of To Catch a Predator ’s blockbuster public-shaming approach. The new movie Primetime , a fictionalized look at the host’s meteoric rise and sudden implosion, also has a critical edge, but it’s much more interested in the weird version of real life that Hansen’s show created. The drama, from the director Lance Oppenheim, plunges the viewer into a sordid vision of early-2000s news entertainment—flashy, shallow, flimsy. And it revolves around an energetic Robert Pattinson performance that always feels a little sweaty and desperate to please the audience. Primetime is a beautiful nightmare—and might feel seductive to anyone who wanted to work in the world of gaudy TV journalism in 2004. That’s when the first To Catch a Predator segment premiered on NBC. It was followed by another, in 2005, before airing as a more regular series from 2006 to 2007. When the program ended, it did so amid a legal accusation of wrongdoing (the case was settled) and questions about its ethics. But during the years it ran, popular culture portrayed Hansen as a righteous crusader. His method—ensnaring alleged sex offenders in online traps meant to expose their dark proclivities, before turning them over to law enforcement—made for satisfying TV, mixing the trashiness of Jerry Springer –style talk shows with the aesthetics of supposed hard-news journalism. [ Read: Jerry Springer explained it all ] Casting Pattinson, a true movie star, as Hansen should stack the deck in the character’s favor: He dazzles on-screen. The actor has long been drawn to playing nervy oddities or handsome devils with some insecurity simmering beneath the surface. He portrays Hansen as sharklike and occasionally charming, unable to drop the facade he’s created for his show. His smirk is frozen, his voice affected. He seems to be constantly preening for cameras that aren’t always there. Pattinson’s performance comes across as fake in just the right ways—it’s an impersonation of someone who was himself living as an impersonator. Oppenheim primarily works as a documentarian, and has long been drawn to the anonymous-feeling tract housing and chintzy suburbs that To Catch a Predator made its domain. His documentary Some Kind of Heaven was about a group of retirees living in The Villages, a master-planned neighborhood for senior citizens; Spermworld explored the unregulated online marketplaces for sperm donation, for which people meet in motels to arrange DIY insemination. In Primetime , the director’s first narrative feature, the Dateline crew infiltrate similar types of communities to wreak gleeful havoc in the name of ratings. But the movie doesn’t condemn their efforts so much as it tries to understand how Hansen’s thirst for success infected everyone around him. (The real Hansen has criticized the film, declaring it “detached from reality.”) The most captivating storyline, in fact, is that of a decoy performer. The aspiring Hollywood actor Dan Plumb (played by Skyler Gisondo) takes the gig because he wants a union card, then quickly finds himself dangled in front of suspected sexual predators with little warning. Gisondo’s performance is as sweet and guileless as Pattinson’s is intense and unsettling; Dan has mighty career ambitions, but he sadly fails to grow beyond his seemingly eternal youth and the specific role Hansen has cast him in. Caught between them is the show’s producer Andie (the incredible Merritt Wever), who suppresses any qualms about her professional ethics in search of the show’s next target. Oppenheim imagines the tale of To Catch a Predator as a story of America. This is apt, considering how many stories about this country involve people pursuing success at any cost—one that typically ends up being very high. Primetime eventually careers toward disaster (drawn from the real-life incident that ended the show’s run), but any viewer can see that coming. More fascinating to behold is Hansen’s delight as he gets closer and closer to that grand catastrophe.

items.title: Elim CAN 2027 : les Lions de l’Atlas s’imposent avec maîtrise face au Gabon
items.description: Pour leur premier match des éliminatoires de la CAN 2027, les Lions de l’Atlas ont dominé le Gabon (2-0), ce vendredi à Rabat. Après une première période largement maîtrisée, marquée par l’ouverture du score de Noussair Mazraoui, le Maroc a résisté au réveil des Panthères avant de sceller sa victoire grâce à Soufiane Rahimi en fin de rencontre. Les hommes de Mohamed Ouahbi ont rapidement pris le contrôle de la rencontre. Avec une possession largement à leur avantage, les Lions ont installé le jeu dans le camp gabonais et multiplié les tentatives pour déstabiliser le bloc adverse. Après plusieurs situations intéressantes, notamment par Azzedine Ounahi et Yassir Zabiri, le Maroc a finalement été récompensé à la 36e minute. C’est Noussair Mazraoui qui a délivré les Lions. Le latéral de Manchester United a profité d’un espace à une vingtaine de mètres du but gabonais avant de se remettre sur son pied droit. Sa frappe puissante, qui a rebondi devant le gardien, a trompé Amonome, coupable d’une intervention mal maîtrisée. نصير مزراوي بهدف رائـــــــــع يمنح منتخبنا الوطني التقدم What a goal by Noussair Mazraoui to give Our National Team the lead #DimaMaghrib pic.twitter.com/HrdiR2QTou — Équipe du Maroc (@EnMaroc) September 25, 2026 Quelques instants avant le but, Gessime s’était également illustré avec un bon ballon, tandis que la défense gabonaise avait dû intervenir in extremis pour empêcher Zabiri de profiter d’un centre en retrait de Maamar. Après avoir regagné les vestiaires avec un avantage d’un but, le Maroc continue de dominer le Gabon au retour des vestiaires. Les Lions de l’Atlas se procurent plusieurs situations, mais restent sous la menace de Panthères qui commencent progressivement à relever la tête. Le Maroc reprend la seconde période avec les mêmes intentions. Dès la 47e minute, Abdessamad Ezzalzouli accélère sur son côté gauche et obtient un corner après une frappe contrée par Do Marcolino. Les Lions continuent de pousser. À la 49e minute, Ayyoub Bouaddi obtient un coup franc intéressant à une vingtaine de mètres après une faute de Kanga. Ezzalzouli se charge ensuite d'un coup franc à la 50e minute, mais sa tentative manque complètement sa cible. Azzedine Ounahi reste l’un des joueurs les plus entreprenants côté marocain. Le Gabon tente néanmoins de sortir davantage de son camp mais le Maroc continue à monopoliser le ballon et tente de trouver la faille pour inscrire un deuxième but. Le rythme change progressivement après l’heure de jeu. Malgré la domination marocaine, les Panthères affichent davantage de combativité et commencent à se montrer plus présentes dans le camp des Lions. Le Maroc continue toutefois à se procurer des occasions. À la 69e minute, Ounahi bénéficie d’une nouvelle situation à environ 25 mètres du but. Seul face au but, le milieu marocain manque cependant complètement sa frappe, le ballon terminant largement au-dessus. Le Mountakhab a fait le break face au Gabon grâce à Soufiane Rahimi à la 84e minute. Alors que les Panthères commençaient à mettre la pression sur les Lions de l’Atlas, l’attaquant marocain est venu offrir un précieux bol d’air à son équipe. 𝗕𝗨𝗨𝗨𝗨𝗨𝗨𝗧 𝗗𝗘 𝗥𝗔𝗛𝗜𝗠𝗜 !!! pic.twitter.com/uE9pPuPaxy — ᴍᴏᴜɴᴛᴀᴋʜᴀʙ ғᴏᴏᴛ (@MountakhabFoot) September 25, 2026 Alors que le Gabon semblait capable de revenir dans la partie, le Maroc a finalement porté le coup décisif. Une réalisation qui récompense les efforts des Lions et leur permet de prendre une avance beaucoup plus confortable lors de ce match éliminatoire de la CAN 2027. items.title: France beat Turkey 1-0 in Zinedine Zidane’s first game as coach
items.description: Kylian Mbappe scored the only goal of the game before having to come off grimacing with a knee injury as France won 1-0 in Turkey in the UEFA Nations League in new coach Zinedine Zidane’s first game in charge on Friday. The Real Madrid superstar was moved out to the left wing by his new coach after being used through the middle of the France attack under former coach Didier Deschamps at the recent World Cup, which he ended as the top scorer with 10 goals. It was from the left that Mbappe, France’s all-time top scorer, notched his 67th international goal, controlling and firing in low at the near post after being set up by Michael Olise. He winced in pain as his teammates came across to celebrate the goal at the Kocaeli Stadium in Izmit, just over 100 kilometres outside Istanbul. Mbappe tried to carry on after receiving treatment, but eventually slumped to the ground and looked concerned as he prodded the outside of his left knee, before walking off to be replaced by Desire Doue. France and Real will now nervously wait to discover the extent of the injury, with Les Bleus playing three more games over the next 10 days before the club season resumes. The sight of his star player and skipper coming off overshadowed Zidane’s first match since being appointed coach in late July on a deal to 2030. The France legend and 1998 World Cup winner is making his return to elite coaching for the first time since his second stint in charge of Madrid ended in 2021. France, beaten in the semi-finals at the World Cup by eventual winners Spain, are in Group A1 of this edition of the Nations League and will now go to Brussels to face Belgium on Monday. Belgium won 2-0 away to Italy on Friday. – Cherki plays – Zidane, whose last match as a player came for France against Italy in the 2006 World Cup final, will then make his home debut as coach against the Italians at the Stade de France next Friday. His first team selection was not dramatically different to the side that regularly played at the World Cup, although Bournemouth’s Adrien Truffert was in at left-back while Manchester City’s Rayan Cherki came into the starting XI. Olise, the Bayern Munich star who lit up the World Cup, was unlucky not to open the scoring late in the first half when his superb strike was tipped over by home goalkeeper Ugurcan Cakir. France goalkeeper Mike Maignan responded at the start of the second half as he tipped over an attempt by Abdulkerim Bardakci for Turkey, who finished bottom of their group at the World Cup despite a 3-2 win over co-hosts the United States. Mbappe’s goal came shortly after, and the visitors later saw Jules Kounde hit the post before Turkey were reduced to 10 men late on. Cakir came flying out of his area to halt Bradley Barcola as the France substitute raced through on goal. German referee Felix Zwayer initially waved play on before undertaking a VAR review after which he decided the goalkeeper had handled the ball, which meant a red card. Turkey, coached by former Italian international Vincenzo Montella, host Italy next on Monday. items.title: Les Etats-Unis affirment leur engagement pour le développement de la région du Sahara sous la souveraineté du Maroc
items.description: Le Secrétaire d’État adjoint américain, Christopher Landau, a affirmé, vendredi à New York, l’engagement des Etats-Unis pour le développement de la région du Sahara sous la souveraineté du Royaume du Maroc. « Nous avons réaffirmé l'amitié séculaire liant nos deux pays ainsi que notre vision commune pour le développement de la région du Sahara et pour une coopération renforcée sous la souveraineté du Maroc sur ce territoire » , a déclaré Landau à la presse à l’issue d’entretiens avec le ministre des Affaires étrangères, de la Coopération africaine et des Marocains résidant à l’étranger, Nasser Bourita, en marge de la 81e session de l'Assemblée générale de l’ONU. A cet égard, le haut responsable américain a souligné que les Etats-Unis ont « hâte d’oeuvrer avec le Maroc et les autres acteurs concernés en vue de résoudre ce conflit une fois pour toutes ». Déplorant que ce différend régional perdure depuis plus de 50 ans, Landau a souligné que « ce statu quo ne peut être maintenu ». Il a également indiqué avoir réaffirmé, lors de cette entrevue, que « la grande amitié de longue date » liant Rabat et Washington « va se poursuivre à l'avenir », se félicitant du fait que les relations entre les États-Unis d'Amérique et le Royaume du Maroc sont à « leur meilleur niveau de tous les temps ». items.title: Burkina/SITHO 2026 : Zoom sur la région du Liptako
items.description: La région du Liptako offre aux visiteurs du Salon international du tourisme et de l'hôtellerie de Ouagadougou (SITHO), une immersion dans l'univers sahélien. Des produits artisanaux aux mets locaux, en passant par les éléments du patrimoine culturel, chaque objet raconte une partie de l'histoire de la région. Comme on le lit sur leur stand, « le Sahel, une terre de souvenirs et de résilience », la région du Liptako ne se présente pas uniquement comme une destination touristique à ne pas manquer. Elle vient aussi raconter son histoire, son identité à travers des objets confectionnés à la main. Sacs et sandales en cuir, porte-monnaie en passant par les vêtements traditionnels faits à base de laine de mouton, ou encore des calebasses, le savoir-faire artisanal de la région du Liptako témoigne de la richesse de la localité à travers les créations. Dans ce stand qui met en lumière les potentialités du Liptako, nous avons été accueillis par Mamadou Boubacar Diallo. Selon lui, derrière ses objets se cache un savoir-faire artisanal transmis de génération en génération. Selon ses dires, les produits artisanaux qui attirent les regards sont fabriqués à la main et portent l'empreinte culturelle de leur région d'origine. C'est d'ailleurs ce qui fait leur particularité. Une authenticité qui constitue, selon l'artisan, l'un des principaux atouts auprès des visiteurs. Dans un monde où tout change à grande vitesse, notre artisan confie que la modernisation n'est pas forcément synonyme d'abandon des pratiques anciennes, mais plutôt un moyen de préserver les modèles traditionnels tout en les adaptant aux goûts et aux besoins des potentiels clients du moment. Aperçu des articles présentés au stand du Liptako « On a des sandales en cuir, des sacs en cuir, des habits comme ce que j'ai portés, des boubous qui sont faits à base de laine de mouton. Il y a beaucoup de choses ici qui représentent notre région. Tout est artisanal et fait à la main. Les temps changent c'est vrai. Mais, il faut garder ce qui était avant, en faisant d'autres modèles pour les besoins de la nouvelle génération », a-t-il expliqué. Autrefois couramment utilisé, Mamadou Boubacar Diallo a également expliqué que certains objets exposés au stand du Liptako sont aujourd'hui méconnus par la nouvelle génération. Ce faisant, le SITHO intervient comme un moyen de faire découvrir le riche patrimoine et le savoir-faire des artisans sahéliens aux visiteurs. Le SITHO est aussi un lieu de partage d'expériences et d'idées. A cet effet, le marchand souligne que le SITHO est plus qu'un espace de vente. Pour lui, la manifestation permet de présenter certes leurs productions mais aussi de rencontrer d'autres artisans venus des différentes régions du Burkina Faso. « Le SITHO, ça ne veut pas dire que c'est seulement le commerce. C'est plus que cela. On rencontre d'autres artisans et on apprend aussi d'eux et même à connaître le Burkina Faso », a-t-il poursuivi. Derrière cette vitrine culturelle, Mamadou Boubacar Diallo confie que la situation sécuritaire a des répercussions sur les activités économiques. Cependant, cela ne constitue pas un frein car leur présence au SITHO traduit une volonté de continuer à promouvoir les potentialités de la région. « Je souhaite que Dieu nous aide à retrouver la paix. Unissons-nous », tel est le souhait de Mamadou Boubacar Diallo, au SITHO 2026 « Nous voyons que ce n'est pas comme avant. Mais il y a quand même un changement car il y a des endroits où ça va. Et si Dieu le veut ça ira », espère-t-il. À côté de l'artisanat, le Liptako entend également faire découvrir ses saveurs. Dans cette région sahélienne, le lait et ses produits dérivés occupent une place importante dans les habitudes alimentaires et dans l'hospitalité. Parmi les spécialités citées par l'artisan, figure notamment le gapal, une préparation à base de lait très appréciée et proposée aux visiteurs en signe de bienvenue. « Lorsque nous recevons un visiteur chez nous, la première des choses, c'est le gapal que nous offrons. C'est ça, la bonne arrivée au Sahel. Après cela, on peut lui donner du lait, ou lui faire du thé », a-t-il fait savoir. À travers son artisanat, sa gastronomie et ses traditions, le Liptako dévoile au SITHO 2026 une partie de son identité. Une identité que les acteurs de la région souhaitent préserver et transmettre, tout en continuant à regarder vers l'avenir. Au-delà de la découverte touristique, leur message est aussi un appel à la paix et à la cohésion. Muriel Dominique Ouédraogo Lefaso.net

items.title: Health Ministry moves to integrate traditional medicine into mainstream healthcare
items.description: The Deputy Minister for Health, Prof. Dr Grace Ayensu-Danquah, has called for greater integration of scientifically validated traditional medicine into Ghana’s mainstream healthcare system. She said traditional medicine, when properly researched, regulated and manufactured to approved standards, could play a significant role in expanding access to safe and quality healthcare. Prof. Ayensu-Danquah made the call when she visited the Centre of Awareness (COA) Research and Manufacturing Company in the Central Region, where she engaged management and staff and inspected the company’s facilities to assess its compliance with Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP). She said Ghana could learn from countries such as China, where traditional and conventional medicine are used alongside each other to complement healthcare delivery. According to her, closer collaboration between the two sectors could help improve healthcare outcomes while ensuring that traditional medicines used by the public meet the required standards for safety, quality and effectiveness. Prof. Ayensu-Danquah said the government’s Free Primary Healthcare programme, which places emphasis on preventive and promotive healthcare, also presented an opportunity to examine how traditional medicine could contribute to the delivery of primary healthcare. She identified non-communicable diseases, including hypertension and diabetes, as areas where traditional medicine could potentially contribute, subject to scientific validation and appropriate regulation. The CEO of COA Manufacturing Company, Prof. (HC) Samuel Ato Duncan, welcomed the government’s efforts to develop the traditional medicine sector to a standard that would enable it to complement national healthcare programmes, including the Free Primary Healthcare initiative. He said the company was undertaking research into the potential health benefits of some of its products, including their possible applications in the management of cancer and viral diseases. Prof. Duncan stressed the importance of continued research and collaboration between traditional medicine practitioners, researchers and government institutions in unlocking the potential of the sector. He said such collaboration could help strengthen the evidence base for traditional medicines and enable the sector to make a greater contribution to healthcare delivery in Ghana. Prof. Ayensu-Danquah said the Ministry of Health would continue to work with relevant stakeholders to strengthen research, quality assurance, manufacturing and regulation within the traditional medicine sector. She said the broader objective was to create a healthcare system in which traditional and conventional medicine could complement each other safely, based on scientific evidence and appropriate regulatory standards.

items.title: Tehran offers US 7-day plan for Hormuz reopening
items.description: Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Friday that Tehran had offered Washington a plan that would see the Strait of Hormuz reopened to maritime navigation within seven days once agreed. Read Also: Iran president says Tehran wants return to memorandum with US Araghchi met for talks on Tuesday with US President Donald Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff, and previously set out conditions for ending the war and reopening the vital energy shipping channel. “Iran has conveyed to the United States, through Qatar, a concrete seven-day plan. If the necessary conditions are met, the strait can be reopened, and normal maritime passage restored within seven days,” Araghchi said at the UN Friday. “The choice now rests with the United States. Iran does not accept coercion, threats, or intimidation, and Iran will not surrender its sovereign rights under pressure. “I can tell you if there is seriousness in the US side to come to a deal and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, everything is now prepared.” Earlier media reports suggest the new plan calls for a cessation of all hostilities in the Middle East for seven days, including in Lebanon. It also reportedly calls for the release of frozen Iranian assets estimated to be worth at least $12 billion, as well as the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil and an end to the US naval blockade of Iran. On the seventh day of the truce, Iran would reopen Hormuz. Hossein Mohebi, a spokesman for the Revolutionary Guards, the ideological arm of Iran’s military, told AFP in an exclusive interview on Tuesday that ending hostilities in Yemen was also among Tehran’s demands. The US and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding in June that aimed to end the war, reopen the strait and launch talks on Iran’s nuclear program. But the deal broke down shortly afterward when Iran fired on commercial ships in Hormuz that it accused of deviating from its approved route through the waterway. Iran requires ships to obtain authorization before passage, citing security and sovereignty reasons. Ships that refuse to comply are regularly targeted, while the United States sporadically bombs Iranian coastal areas in retaliation. items.title: Procès du crash du vol Air Algérie AH5017 : Le délibéré du Tribunal Correctionnel de Paris attendu le 28 septembre 2026
items.description: Douze ans après le crash dramatique du vol Air Algérie AH5017 dans le désert malien ayant coûté la vie à 116 personnes, le marathon judiciaire touche à sa fin. Jugée en mars 2026 devant le Tribunal Correctionnel de Paris pour homicides involontaires, la compagnie aérienne espagnole Swiftair connaîtra son jugement le 28 septembre 2026 à 10h00. Alors que le Ministère public a réclamé la peine maximale de 225 000 euros d'amende, les familles de victimes, notamment au Burkina Faso et en France, retiennent leur souffle dans l'attente d'une décision historique. Le 24 juillet 2014, le vol AH5017 reliant Ouagadougou à Alger s'écrase dans une zone désertique du nord du Mali, ne laissant aucun survivant parmi les 116 passagers et membres d'équipage. L'appareil, un McDonnell Douglas MD-83 affrété par Air Algérie, était opéré avec son équipage par la compagnie charter espagnole Swiftair. Parmi les victimes figuraient 54 citoyens français et 23 ressortissants burkinabè, plongeant plusieurs nations dans le deuil et marquant le début d'un long combat pour la vérité. Au cours des audiences tenues en mars 2026 devant le Tribunal Correctionnel de Paris, les débats se sont focalisés sur la responsabilité pénale de Swiftair. L'accusation et les expertises techniques du Bureau d'enquêtes et d'analyses (BEA) ont mis en lumière les défaillances imputables à l'exploitant espagnol. Les investigations ont révélé que l'accident était survenu à la suite d'un givrage des capteurs de vitesse (sondes Pitot) lors du traversement d'une zone orageuse, entraînant un ralentissement non détecté des moteurs. Au tribunal, les débats ont rigoureusement interrogé le niveau de formation et d'entraînement des pilotes et copilotes saisonniers mobilisés par Swiftair. Le Parquet a soutenu l'existence d'un lien de causalité direct entre les lacunes de préparation de l'équipage face aux situations critiques de givrage et la perte de contrôle fatale de l'aéronef. À l'issue des réquisitions présentées le 25 mars 2026, le Ministère public a demandé la reconnaissance formelle de la responsabilité pénale de la compagnie Swiftair. Le Parquet a requis la condamnation de l'entreprise au paiement d'une amende de 225 000 euros, soit la peine financière maximale prévue par la loi pour des faits d'homicides involontaires commis par une personne morale. De son côté, la défense de la compagnie espagnole a plaidé la relaxe tout au long du procès. Pour les familles réunies au sein des associations de victimes — tant en France qu'au Burkina Faso, où une stèle commémorative rappelle le souvenir des disparus —, ce délibéré représente l'aboutissement d'un parcours du combattant judiciaire de plus d'une décennie. La décision, qui sera lue le 28 septembre 2026 à 10h00 par le Tribunal Correctionnel de Paris, est attendue comme un acte fondateur de justice et de dignité pour la mémoire des 116 disparus. items.title: Iran president says Tehran wants return to memorandum with US
items.description: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said on Friday that his country wanted to return to the memorandum of understanding agreed with the United States in June, days after saying his country would not bend to Washington. He welcomed China saying it wanted the agreement to be revived, posting on X that “Iran shares this approach and underscores the importance of returning to that understanding”. Diplomatic efforts to bring an end to the Middle East war, launched by the US and Israel with surprise attacks on Iran in late February, have faltered for months. The June deal aimed to lay the ground for a full peace deal but it quickly unravelled. There had been optimism that talks might be revived during the UN General Assembly this week, but in a defiant speech to the world body on Wednesday, Pezeshkian said Iran would not “bend at the knee” to the US. A day later he told Fox News that Iran did “not wish to continue” the war but it was up to Washington to end it. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi took part in a meeting with US envoy Steve Witkoff and presidential son-in-law Jared Kushner on the sidelines of the General Assembly, but their talks did not immediately yield a breakthrough. items.title: 550 pupils in Kintampo South get educational lifeline as ‘Seeds of Hope’ reaches farming communities
items.description: More than 550 pupils in two farming communities in the Kintampo South District have received school supplies as part of an outreach programme aimed at easing some of the educational challenges confronting children in rural Ghana. The intervention formed part of the 2026 “Seeds of Hope” Community Outreach and School Donation Campaign by SeedSpark Foundation, in partnership with Legacy Impact through the Legacy Career Institute and OhenebaCare Foundation. The school gates in Anokyekrom and Abom Komkomba had barely opened on Monday, September 21, 2026, when the communities began buzzing with activity. Volunteers were setting up, health workers were preparing for free screening, and boxes of books and other educational materials were being arranged for pupils. For the children, however, the excitement was about more than a change from the usual school routine. They were about to receive some of the basic items many of them need to participate fully in the classroom. A total of 250 pupils in Anokyekrom and 300 in Abom Komkomba, from Kindergarten through Junior High School, received exercise books, textbooks, pens, pencils, rulers, school bags, clothing and footballs. The schools also received textbooks and Teaching and Learning Materials for use by teachers. For some teachers, the donation addresses a challenge that is familiar in many rural classrooms — trying to deliver lessons with limited teaching and learning resources. A teacher at Abom Komkomba D/A School welcomed the intervention, saying the textbooks would support both teachers and pupils. “The textbooks we’ve received will help us study and teach the kids,” she said. She added that some pupils regularly report to school without exercise books, making the donation particularly important. “This will help them and make learning and teaching enjoyable and easier. God bless SeedSpark Foundation,” she said. Executive Director of SeedSpark Foundation, Henry Ekow Yawson, said the organisation deliberately focuses on farming communities, where children can sometimes have fewer educational resources despite their communities playing an important role in Ghana’s food production. “Communities like Anokyekrom and Abom Komkomba are the backbone of this country’s food supply, yet their children are often the last to receive the tools they need to learn,” he said. According to him, the Foundation intends to continue returning to such communities because educational opportunity should not depend on where a child is born. “Every child deserves a fair shot, no matter where they’re born,” he added. The organisers say the intervention was designed to go beyond a one-day distribution exercise. Director of Legacy Impact, David, spoke to the pupils about opportunities available through the Legacy Career Institute and encouraged them to remain committed to their education. He said the objective was to help the children understand that their current circumstances do not have to define the limits of their future. “We don’t just want to hand out books and leave. We want these children to know that there’s a path beyond this classroom,” he said. Volunteers also spent time with the pupils, engaging them through games, singing and conversations. For the organisers, those interactions were just as important as the physical donations because they created an opportunity to encourage the children directly. The outreach also brought healthcare services closer to residents. An 18-member medical team comprising personnel from Kintampo South Hospital, OhenebaCare Foundation and the National Health Insurance Scheme screened an estimated 160 residents. The NHIS component was particularly targeted at helping residents understand and access the scheme while ensuring farmers who needed registration or renewal support could receive it during the outreach. Organisers plan to expand the campaign to more communities and undertake follow-up visits. Those visits are expected to help identify and respond to some of the needs uncovered during the education and health activities. By the end of the day, the classrooms at Anokyekrom and Abom Komkomba had gained new teaching materials, hundreds of pupils had received school supplies and dozens of residents had accessed health services. But for SeedSpark Foundation and its partners, the campaign represents something broader than a single day’s activities. It is an attempt to put practical resources behind a simple proposition: that a child’s access to education should not be determined by whether they grow up in a farming community or a major urban centre. The Foundation says the work will continue under its guiding motto: “Seeds of Change, Sprout of Success.”

items.title: Dr Gorgui Diouf : « Un monde où 1,4 milliard d’Africains n’ont pas de voix permanente est profondément injuste »
items.description: Alors que se déroule la 81e session de l’Assemblée générale des Nations unies, sur fond de conflits persistants et de rivalités entre grandes puissances, Gorgui Diouf, Docteur en Droit public, spécialiste du droit international public, des relations internationales et de la géopolitique, également expert du droit onusien, porte un regard critique sur l’état du multilatéralisme. Dans cet entretien, il analyse les limites du système des Nations unies, la paralysie du Conseil de sécurité, les enjeux de sa réforme et la recomposition des rapports de force mondiaux. La 81e Assemblée générale de l’Onu s’ouvre dans un contexte de conflits multiples et de tensions entre grandes puissances. Quel état du monde cette rencontre va-t-elle, selon vous, mettre en lumière ? Cette 81e Assemblée générale des Nations unies va mettre en lumière un monde qui a perdu ses repères juridiques et moraux. Nous assistons à une forme de régression du droit international public. Les grands principes qui fondaient l’ordre mondial depuis 1945, tels que la sécurité collective et le règlement pacifique des différends (le chapitre VI et les articles 33 et 38 de la Charte), ainsi que l’interdiction du recours à la force (article 2, paragraphe 4), sont aujourd’hui piétinés par ceux-là mêmes qui devraient en être les garants. Le Conseil de sécurité est devenu le théâtre d’une confiscation de l’autorité juridique de l’Onu par les cinq membres permanents. Chacun utilise le droit de veto non pas pour protéger la paix, mais pour protéger ses intérêts géostratégiques. Résultat : les conflits comme celui du Sahel, du Soudan ou de l’est de la République démocratique du Congo s’enlisent et l’Onu assiste, impuissante, à la décomposition de régions entières. Cette Assemblée générale sera donc le miroir d’un monde où le droit n’est plus qu’un instrument au service de la puissance. Face à la multiplication des crises et aux difficultés du Conseil de sécurité, l’Onu dispose-t-elle encore des moyens politiques nécessaires pour peser réellement sur les grands conflits internationaux ? La réponse est non et il faut avoir le courage de le dire. L’Onu ne dispose plus des moyens politiques de sa mission parce que sa structure même est viciée à la racine. Dans le cadre de mes recherches, j’ai analysé en profondeur ce que j’appelle la « tare congénitale » du système onusien. La Charte de San Francisco a été rédigée en 1945 par les vainqueurs de la Seconde Guerre mondiale pour un monde qui n’existe plus. Elle n’a jamais prévu les conflits armés internes, les guerres civiles, les rébellions, les formes de terrorisme qui déchirent l’Afrique. L’Onu a dû bricoler des opérations de maintien de la paix qui n’ont aucune base juridique explicite dans la Charte. Et aujourd’hui, ces bricolages montrent leurs limites. Le Conseil de sécurité est paralysé par le veto. L’Assemblée générale est réduite à des recommandations sans force contraignante. Le Secrétaire général est un géant politique aux mains liées. L’Onu n’est pas impuissante par accident ; elle est impuissante par construction. Et cette impuissance est encore plus criante en Afrique où les conflits internes sont complexes, imprévisibles et où les puissances n’ont souvent aucun intérêt stratégique à agir. La réforme du Conseil de sécurité revient régulièrement. Peut-on s’attendre à des avancées concrètes, notamment en ce qui concerne la représentation de l’Afrique ? Il faut être lucide : il n’y aura pas d’avancée majeure cette année ni l’année prochaine. Les cinq membres permanents ne renonceront jamais volontairement à leur privilège. Le droit de veto est pour eux un attribut de souveraineté, un instrument de domination. L’Afrique le réclame depuis des décennies, mais elle se heurte à un mur. Cela dit, cette Assemblée générale est une occasion de plus pour le Sénégal et pour l’Union africaine de poser le problème en termes de justice et non de simple réforme technique. Il ne s’agit pas seulement de savoir qui siège au Conseil, mais de quel monde nous voulons. Un monde où 1,4 milliard d’Africains n’ont pas de voix permanente au Conseil de sécurité est un monde profondément injuste. Et cette injustice est une cause directe de l’instabilité sur notre continent. Tant que l’Afrique ne sera pas représentée dignement, les décisions sur la paix en Afrique seront prises sans les Africains et souvent contre eux. Dans un contexte de rivalités croissantes entre puissances occidentales, Chine, Russie et pays du Sud global, assiste-t-on à une recomposition durable des rapports de force au sein des Nations unies ? Oui, nous assistons à une recomposition historique. Le monde unipolaire dominé par les États-Unis est en train de céder la place à un monde multipolaire où la Chine, la Russie, l’Inde, le Brésil et les pays du Sud global pèsent de plus en plus. Mais, attention : multipolarité ne signifie pas automatiquement paix ou justice. Le risque, c’est que cette recomposition se fasse dans la confrontation, dans une nouvelle guerre froide qui utiliserait l’Afrique comme terrain d’affrontement. Le Sénégal, comme la plupart des pays africains, refuse d’être un pion dans ce jeu. Nous devons être des acteurs, pas des enjeux. C’est pourquoi la diplomatie sénégalaise doit être audacieuse, non alignée, mais pas neutre. Non alignée sur les blocs, mais fermement engagée pour le droit international, pour la justice et pour la paix. Au-delà de la paix et de la sécurité, le climat, le financement du développement et la gouvernance de l’Intelligence artificielle sont à l’agenda. Quels résultats concrets les pays africains peuvent-ils attendre ? Les attentes sont immenses, mais les résultats seront probablement décevants. Sur le climat, l’Afrique subit de plein fouet les conséquences d’un réchauffement qu’elle n’a pas causé. Les promesses de financement ne sont pas tenues. Sur le développement, l’architecture financière internationale est conçue pour maintenir les pays africains dans une dépendance structurelle. Sur l’Intelligence artificielle, l’Afrique risque d’être un simple marché pour les technologies des autres, sans maîtrise ni régulation. Toutefois, il y a une chose que les pays africains peuvent et doivent faire : exiger que ces questions soient traitées dans une logique de justice globale et non de charité. Le Sénégal doit porter une voix forte pour un financement climatique juste, pour une réforme de la gouvernance économique mondiale et pour une gouvernance de l’IA qui protège les droits humains et la souveraineté des peuples. Ces combats sont indissociables de la paix. Pour le Sénégal, quelles devraient être les priorités diplomatiques à cette tribune et quelle place le pays peut-il occuper dans les débats sur la réforme de la gouvernance mondiale ? Le Sénégal a une carte à jouer et il doit la jouer avec intelligence et courage. Sa première priorité, c’est de porter la voix de l’Afrique pour la réforme du Conseil de sécurité. Le Sénégal a une légitimité historique : il est un pays stable, démocratique, respecté, qui a toujours contribué aux opérations de maintien de la paix. Il doit être le fer de lance de cette bataille pour la justice institutionnelle. La deuxième priorité consiste à proposer une nouvelle approche de la sécurité au Sahel. Le Sénégal doit plaider pour une stratégie qui ne soit pas uniquement militaire, mais qui s’attaque aux causes profondes, à savoir la pauvreté, l’exclusion, le manque d’éducation. La troisième priorité, et c’est la plus profonde, est de faire du Sénégal le laboratoire d’une culture de la paix en Afrique. Le Sénégal a une richesse inestimable : sa culture de dialogue, de tolérance. Notre pays a une histoire de médiation, de dialogue pacifique. Il doit transformer cette richesse en une véritable diplomatie culturelle de la paix. Concrètement, cela signifie investir massivement dans l’éducation à la paix, dans la formation des jeunes, dans la promotion des valeurs de non-violence. « La paix ne se décrète pas à New York ; elle se construit dans les esprits », dans les écoles, dans les villages. Le Sénégal peut et doit être le pionnier de cette approche. · Entretien réalisé par Daouda DIOUF

items.title: Affaire une tombe profanée à Karangasso-Sambla pour « libérer la pluie » parce la défunte n’avait pas de seins: La dépouille introuvable, le dossier sans suite
items.description: Dans la commune de Karangasso-Sambla, située dans la province du Houet, une affaire de profanation de sépulture d'une gravité exceptionnelle plonge les habitants dans un vif émoi. Exhumée au motif irrationnel que son absence de poitrine de son vivant bloquait le retour des pluies, la dépouille mortelle d'une femme est aujourd'hui portée disparue après avoir été déplacée de site en site. Selon les faits révélés par le quotidien L'Express du Faso , le dossier transmis au Service Régional de la Police Judiciaire reste sans suite, laissant la famille de la défunte dans l'humiliation et menaçant d'enflammer les tensions communautaires. Tout a basculé au cœur de la commune de Karangasso-Sambla à la suite d'une vague de sécheresse que certains habitants ont choisi d'imputer à des causes mystiques. Ciblant la sépulture récente d'une femme du village au motif que celle-ci « n'avait pas poussé des seins » de son vivant, des individus ont entrepris de profaner sa tombe. Convaincus que sa morphologie faisait obstacle à la pluie sur le site où elle reposait, les profanateurs ont exhumé la dépouille au mépris des contestations farouches de ses descendants. Une fois extraite de sa sépulture, la dépouille mortelle a été soumise à une errance clandestine avant d'être totalement perdue de vue. Comme le rapporte L'Express du Faso , le corps a d'abord été déposé au bord d'un premier cours d'eau, puis transporté et abandonné sur les berges d'un second point d'eau. Par la suite, les auteurs de l'acte l'ont emporté vers une destination inconnue, vraisemblablement dans une forêt située sur le territoire d'un village lointain. Aujourd'hui, l'incertitude est totale : ni les parents de la défunte, ni même les personnes ayant exécuté l'exhumation ne savent où repose exactement le corps. Pour la famille victime, contrainte de subir quotidiennement toutes formes d'humiliations et de pressions, le choc est immense. Leur seule exigence demeure de pouvoir localiser les restes de leur parente afin de lui offrir enfin un repos digne. Afin d'enrayer l'escalade et préserver la cohésion sociale, les autorités administratives et coutumières se sont impliquées localement pour trouver une médiation et renforcer le vivre-ensemble. Cependant, ces démarches d'apaisement peinent à porter leurs fruits face au refus de restituer le corps et de faire la lumière sur cet outrage. Sur le plan judiciaire, le dossier a été confié au Service Régional de la Police Judiciaire (SRPJ). Bien que des auditions de témoins et de suspects aient eu lieu dans les premiers jours de l'enquête, la procédure est depuis lors au point mort, suscitant l'incompréhension générale. Sans réponse de la justice et face à cette impunité apparente, la cohésion communautaire vole en éclats, faisant peser un risque imminent d'affrontement entre les deux familles désormais ouvertement opposées au sein du village.
