items.title: Fonsis : le Fonds islamique de Relance injecte 600 millions FCFA dans quatre entreprises
items.description: Le Fonds islamique de Relance (FIR), filiale du Fonds souverain d’investissements stratégiques (Fonsis), poursuit son accompagnement des entreprises sénégalaises. Il a formalisé, mardi 22 septembre, un investissement global de 600 millions de FCFA au profit de quatre entreprises opérant dans l’agroalimentaire, l’agro-industrie et l’enseignement scientifique. Les bénéficiaires sont Agro Industries du Nord (AIN), Mintou Rassoul, Bassari Baobab et l’École scientifique internationale d’Excellence (ESIEX). Réparties entre Saint-Louis, Tambacounda, Dakar et Keur Massar, ces structures bénéficieront de financements en fonds propres destinés notamment à moderniser leurs outils de production, renforcer leurs capacités de stockage et d’approvisionnement et développer de nouvelles infrastructures éducatives. Renforcer la filière rizicole Dans la vallée du fleuve Sénégal, le FIR accompagne deux entreprises engagées dans la filière rizicole. Implantée à Ross-Béthio, Agro Industries du Nord transforme le riz paddy dans une unité disposant d’une capacité de décorticage de trois tonnes par heure. Son investissement sera consacré à l’installation d’équipements solaires et à l’augmentation de ses capacités de stockage, avec l’objectif de mieux sécuriser son approvisionnement. De son côté, Mintou Rassoul, basée dans la région de Saint-Louis, produit, transforme et commercialise du riz blanc et du riz étuvé ainsi que différents sous-produits de transformation. La modernisation de son unité doit permettre d’améliorer la qualité de ses produits et d’augmenter les volumes de production. À travers ces deux opérations, le FIR entend contribuer au développement de la production et de la transformation locales du riz, tout en soutenant l’emploi dans la vallée du fleuve Sénégal et en renforçant l’offre nationale face aux importations. Le pari sur les produits agroforestiers À Tambacounda, l’investissement concerne Bassari Baobab, une entreprise spécialisée dans la valorisation de produits agroforestiers locaux, notamment le baobab, le bissap et le gingembre. Commercialisés sous les marques Zahra et Mouna, ces produits bénéficieront d’un renforcement des capacités de l’entreprise à travers la modernisation de ses équipements et la mise à niveau de ses espaces de production et de stockage. L’entreprise compte actuellement 60 employés, dont une majorité de femmes. Pour le FIR, cette opération illustre également sa volonté d’élargir l’accès à ses solutions de financement aux petites et moyennes entreprises sur l’ensemble du territoire national. Un investissement dans la formation scientifique Le quatrième bénéficiaire est l’École scientifique internationale d’Excellence (ESIEX), créée en 2019 au sein du Groupe Supdeco. L’établissement, implanté à Dakar, assure une formation allant du secondaire aux classes préparatoires et prépare ses élèves aux concours des grandes écoles d’ingénieurs. Le financement du FIR doit permettre d’équiper son futur campus de Keur Massar, de développer ses laboratoires et d’acquérir du matériel destiné à l’enseignement scientifique. Pour Abdoul Aziz Sy, PDG du Groupe Supdeco, cet appui répond à un enjeu stratégique pour le Sénégal : renforcer la formation de scientifiques et préparer les compétences dont le pays aura besoin dans les prochaines années. 7,5 milliards FCFA d’investissements cumulés Avec cette nouvelle opération, le FIR franchit un nouveau palier. Selon Babacar Gning, directeur général du Fonsis, le montant cumulé des investissements réalisés par le fonds, sous forme de fonds propres et de prêts Moudharaba, atteint désormais 7,5 milliards de FCFA. Pour Adramé Ndione, directeur du FIR, l’objectif est de proposer des solutions de financement à des entreprises de secteurs et de profils différents, en les rendant accessibles aux PME partout au Sénégal, au plus près de leurs activités et de leurs besoins. Filiale du Fonsis issue d’un partenariat entre le Fonsis, la Banque islamique de développement et l’État du Sénégal, le Fonds islamique de Relance dispose d’une enveloppe de 20 milliards de FCFA. Il propose aux PME des solutions de financement fondées sur des instruments de finance islamique afin d’accompagner la relance et le développement de leurs activités.

items.title: What Does the Climate Movement Do Now?
items.description: The day the Biden administration celebrated the first major piece of climate legislation in U.S. history, the weather happened to be sublime. The White House’s South Lawn, a billiard-table green, stretched out beneath a cerulean sky. Ben Beachy, who served as a special assistant to President Biden and would help oversee the law’s implementation, told me that “it felt like the dawn of a new era.” The Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 was set to deliver hundreds of billions of dollars in federal investments to clean-energy programs, and to those partying in Washington, the law was a major step toward a long-sought goal: a plan for America’s future that addressed the realities of climate change. Four years on, the Republican Congress has mostly dismantled the IRA, electric-vehicle sales are in a slump, and the Trump administration is accelerating oil and gas development while axing environmental protections. The U.S. climate movement, Beachy said, “is currently experiencing a bout of dysphoria.” That’s putting it lightly. Longtime allies in the Democratic Party seem to be losing interest. Corporate America has all but ghosted climate advocates after making big pledges to go greener. Philanthropic support has gone squishy. Meanwhile, the planet is on track to speed past a 1.5-degree-Celsius increase in average global temperatures, the threshold that has been considered the bright line of danger since the Paris Agreement. Climate leaders have sought to project a keep-calm-and-carry-on attitude. “I would characterize this moment in time as just a moment in time,” Michael Brune, the former head of the Sierra Club and the CEO of the Clean Break Fund , told me. This is just an ebb tide, advocates insist, not all that different from past periods when climate slipped to the margins of the political conversation. There’s no doubt, however, that the dysphoria is real. I spoke with more than a dozen climate leaders spanning the academic, advocacy, and philanthropic sectors who told me, in different ways, that the American climate movement is unsure where to go from here. Having sunk to such lows so soon after climbing to such great heights, climate activists are scrambling to find the movement’s next big idea—some path that will lead them back out of the political wilderness. But right now they’re lost. If the Inflation Reduction Act managed to be one of the most tepidly—and confusingly—titled laws in American history, it also represented a genuine breakthrough for climate action, an opportunity to begin reorganizing the U.S. economy around climate goals. Previously, the climate movement had two strategic strands, broadly speaking. The first focused on policy: pushing for international agreements (such as the Kyoto Protocol, which was never ratified) and national laws that would limit greenhouse-gas emissions (such as the Obama-era cap-and-trade bill that died in the Senate). Advocates scored their clearest win in 2015 with the signing of the Paris Agreement—though the signatories have failed to meet the accord’s lofty goals. The second strategy was to attack fossil fuels directly, along with the financial institutions underwriting them. The movement had some victories: The Keystone XL pipeline died; hundreds of U.S. colleges and churches divested from fossil-fuel companies; coal plants across the country were scheduled for closure. Then came the Green New Deal and its vision of an American manufacturing renaissance. After the neoliberal consensus that markets could manage carbon emissions fell apart, advocates and their allies in the Democratic Party got behind the idea that the best way to ratchet down emissions would be to build things: solar farms, electric-vehicle factories, high-speed rail. It was technocratic, sure, but also bold, a callback to the FDR era. Under industrial policy, the invisible hand of the market would be enclosed in a tight glove of federal priority-setting. The now-deflated Inflation Reduction Act was the wonky and somewhat less bold version of this ambition. Today, the overriding theory of change remains the same as ever: Back fossil fuels into the grave and drive a transition to renewable energy marked by speed and scale. But within the movement, there’s little consensus on how to do that. The climate movement does not lack for clever proposals—state-level cap-and-invest programs, grid modernization, make-polluters-pay laws, greater investments in climate-change adaptation. What it lacks is support that’s as resolute as it is broad. This has always been the climate movement’s Achilles’ heel, even at the high-water mark of the Greta Thunberg–inspired school strikes and mass marches in the years leading up to the pandemic. Climate change doesn’t score well on what public-opinion pollsters call “salience.” A majority of Americans are worried about climate change; in fact, the number of people who say they are concerned is near an all-time high . But when asked to rank climate change among other issues such as the cost of living, immigration, and health care, it turns out that most Americans aren’t very worried. This is a structural hurdle. For decades, climate advocates have anchored their efforts in grand ideals of generational responsibility, international solidarity, and care for other species. Although inspiring, those ideals might also sound— how to put this? —abstract. So, desperate for a way to connect with Americans and their immediate concerns, climate-movement leaders are searching for some political wave to surf. The most talked-about notion for a climate-action banner is the same issue everyone seems to be talking about: affordability. In this, the climate movement has a new ally—economics. As recently as a decade ago, “wind and solar were not cheaper. Period. Full stop,” Pete Maysmith, the president of the League of Conservation Voters, told me. “There were a bunch of reasons to do it, but it wasn’t affordability.” Now solar-plus-battery storage has become the cheapest form of new energy generation, as well as the quickest to build. Despite President Trump’s attacks on wind power, more than 90 percent of new electricity capacity that came online in the U.S. in 2025 was from renewables. That technological and market reality means that advocates can argue, for really the first time, that a clean-energy transition is good, not just for the planet, but also for pocketbooks. This is especially true as Trump’s war against Iran spikes household energy costs. The hope among advocates is that solar, batteries, and wind can go from being coded as liberal to being coded simply as cheap—the Costco of energy as opposed to the Whole Foods of energy, as Bill McKibben likes to say. This emphasis on cheap, clean energy is mostly a messaging strategy, but it does have real potential as policy. Environmental groups have used the clean-as-cheap argument to push public utilities commissions to approve renewable-energy projects , and Democrats in Congress have floated legislation, such as the Energy Bills Relief Act , that seeks to use the affordability argument to revive portions of the doomed IRA. But some climate advocates caution, usually off the record, that crowing about how cheap clean energy is risks overpromising. Even a full utility-sector embrace of renewables is unlikely to cut most Americans’ monthly bills in the short run, and will merely slow the projected increase in costs. “Cost plateau” is a tough political sell, and recent polling suggests that the clean-as-cheap message isn’t breaking through. So many climate advocates are looking to hitch the clean-energy future to populist concerns about AI, which is driving U.S. energy-demand growth and, in case you missed it, is strikingly unpopular. Some climate leaders think the AI boom could be a way to underwrite the transition to renewables. “We’re going to make the hyperscalers pay for it, and that’s what I think is going to likely catch on with Democratic presidential candidates,” John Podesta, a consigliere to the last three Democratic presidents and a longtime climate-action champion, told me. BeYONCE is the cringeworthy acronym for this idea—bring your own clean energy. A parallel notion is to force the AI giants to offset their electricity guzzling by paying for household energy upgrades—putting heat pumps in every home in exchange for being allowed to build data centers But that would ultimately ally the climate movement to one of the least popular industries in America. A community that is organizing to stop an AI data center because of its impact on local landscapes or the area’s rural character is unlikely to change positions because the AI facility comes with a giant solar farm. And for more radical climate activists, the notion of getting cozy with the AI bros raises major red flags. Aru Shiney-Ajay, the executive director of the Sunrise Movement, the youth-led climate group that helped popularize the Green New Deal, floated the idea that challenging AI build-out could be a political bank shot. She’s less interested in using the AI boom to also build renewable energy—à la Podesta—than she is in exploring whether antipathy to the tech giants can be married to antipathy to oil giants. “It’s basically a question of whether or not corporations get to control the land and the air and water around us, or whether ordinary people get to,” she told me. Leah Stokes, a professor of political science at UC Santa Barbara and the author of the new book The Carbon Wave , also proposed a political bank shot—connecting high energy costs and the data-center blowback to anger with Trump-administration corruption. Frustration with elites and “throw the bums out” populism could, in theory, lead some people to focus on the profiteering, and the massive political influence, of oil and gas companies. “People don’t like fossil-fuel companies,” Stokes told me. “It’s quite intuitive for a normal person to understand that those people are profiting and making billions while the rest of America can’t even pay their energy bills.” The climate leaders I talked with believe that Americans are thinking about climate change differently these days. They have a clearer understanding that it is contributing to painful increases in grocery costs and beginning to directly weigh on some families’ most valuable asset—their home; as homeowners in disaster-prone areas of California, Florida, and Louisiana are finding it more difficult to get insurance. It is time, some climate advocates believe, for a wholesale pivot from a morally centered movement to one centered on people’s material conditions—to reframe climate change as a kitchen-table issue for the first time. “You’ve never had more people who are experiencing climate change as a reality, not as a future problem,” Abigail Dillen, the president of Earthjustice, an environmental-law nonprofit, told me. “Real people at actual kitchen tables are talking about extreme heat, extreme weather, the insurance crisis.” Real talk among real people is, no doubt, essential for any political movement. It’s also insufficient. If a climate message begins with energy affordability or the simmering insurance crisis or the health impacts of wildfire smoke, it then needs to build to the ultimate goal of limiting carbon pollution, whether through the supply-side strategy of stopping future oil and gas projects or through the demand-side tactic of installing more solar panels that are hooked up to EVs. Perhaps that’s a bridge too far? The climate movement’s best ideas these days are little more than communication plays. The movement has a pile of white papers big enough to practically fuel a power plant’s boiler. But nearly 40 years after the NASA scientist James Hansen warned Congress of the dangers of global warming, a brutal mismatch exists between the number of Americans for whom climate change is priority No. 1 and the scale of the task at hand. All political movements go through times of boom and bust, and even the bust moments can be a fertile time for experimentation and visioning. On that point, Beachy, the former Biden-administration official, likes to quote (with no small amount of ironic self-knowing) the advice of the arch free-market fundamentalist Milton Friedman, to keep developing alternatives to favorite policies, “until the politically impossible becomes the politically inevitable.” Inevitable, though, can take an awfully long while to arrive, and addressing climate change is, infamously, a timed test. Despite its many bright ideas, the one thing the climate movement doesn’t have is time.

items.title: Keïtayah : un présumé malfaiteur interpellé en flagrant délit lors du vandalisme d’une boutique
items.description: Dans le cadre de la lutte contre le grand banditisme, le Secrétariat général à la Présidence, chargé de la lutte contre le crime organisé, a procédé à l’interpellation d’un présumé malfaiteur, surpris en flagrant délit de vandalisme dans une boutique située à Keïtayah, dans la nuit. Le nommé Amara Bangoura, ferrailleur de profession, présenté ce vendredi 25 septembre 2026 à Kaloum, a reconnu les faits qui lui sont reprochés, notamment un vol aggravé commis de nuit et en bande, avec escalade, effraction et pénétration dans une boutique après déchirure des tôles. Des faits prévus et punis par les dispositions de l’article 374 et suivants du Code pénal. S’exprimant sur instruction du Secrétaire général et avec l’approbation du procureur, le commissaire principal de police Foromo Soropogui est revenu sur le mode opératoire des présumés malfaiteurs : « Les Services Spéciaux vous présente ce matin un bandit, d'apparence trompeuse et d'une dangerosité mystique opérant en groupe de trois éléments. Dans la nuit du 02 septembre 2026 aux environs de 4 heures du matin, les nommés Amara BANGOURA alias « Makalos », un second surnommé « Gniné » et le troisième « Papis » sont parti à Keïtayah dans le domicile d'un Citoyen, au moment pluvieux, escalader le mur, puis pénétrer dans la boutique par effraction: c’est-à-dire usage de ciseau et marteau pour déchirer la tôle et le plafond. Ouvrir la porte, transporter et stocker dans les herbes à 60 mètres de la scène de crime, des marchandises diverses et numéraires». Le commissaire principal de la Direction centrale de la lutte contre le crime organisé a poursuivi : «Faits constatés par les habitants voisins très solidaires, et avec l'intervention rapide d'une équipe des services spéciaux, l'un des malfrats fût arrêté et mis à notre disposition. Les marchandises volées furent récupérées, sauf le montant de 3.750.000 francs guinéens emportés par « Gninè » et « Papis » en fuite. À en croire ce responsable des Services spéciaux, les deux autres mis en cause seraient des habitués des juridictions : «Gninè » et «Papis » sont des récidivistes déférés au tribunal de Dubréka en début de cette année», a-t-il rappelé. Devant les caméras et les micros, le présumé délinquant Amara Bangoura, interpellé par les agents des Services spéciaux, a reconnu les faits qui lui sont reprochés, en ces termes : « Je reconnu les faits. On était trois mais moi je connais pas là-bas, moi, c’est mon grand qui est venu me dire de l'accompagner, je ne savais pas qu’on partait ici. On est venu jusqu'à cet endroit comme il ne voulais que je sache ce qu’il veux faire, il m'a dit de m'arrêter au carrefour là-bas je me suis arrêté au Carrefour et eux ils sont descendu en bas. Quelques temps après j’ai vu grand Papis transporter des colis et les amener vers moi et m’ont dit maintenant on va les transporter à la maison, je lui ait dit non, je ne peux pas le faire car je suis malade je ne vais pas transporter les colis», a-t-il déclaré, tout en soulignant qu’il s’agissait, selon lui, de sa première participation à ce type d’opération. Mamadou Yaya Barry L’article Keïtayah : un présumé malfaiteur interpellé en flagrant délit lors du vandalisme d’une boutique est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: Téléphone aux toilettes : quand le petit écran fait durer la pause
items.description: Aux toilettes aussi, le smartphone semble avoir trouve sa place. a Bamako, certains ne s'y rendent plus sans leur telephone, histoire de repondre a un message, scroller sur les reseaux sociaux ou simplement passer le temps. Une habitude parfois amusante pour ceux qui la pratiquent, mais beaucoup moins pour ceux qui attendent derriere la porte. Et selon des medecins, prolonger son sejour aux toilettes n'est pas non plus sans consequences pour la sante. Dans certaines familles et meme sur certains lieux de travail, voir une personne entrer aux toilettes avec son telephone n'a plus rien d'exceptionnel. Pour certains, cette pratique est devenue une veritable habitude. « Je me sens a l'aise dans les toilettes avec mon telephone. C'est devenu comme une addiction, je ne peux pas m'en empecher » , temoigne Samba Diallo. Fatimata Maïga, elle, en parle avec le sourire : « ca a un goût inexplicable. » Elle reconnaît toutefois qu'il vaut mieux eviter d'en faire une habitude. Pour d'autres, le reflexe remonte a l'enfance. Un interlocuteur qui prefere rester anonyme, que nous appellerons Moussa, raconte avoir ete inspire par son grand-pere. « Lorsqu'on etait petit, il rentrait tres souvent avec sa radio pour ecouter les informations. J'ai pris ca comme une bonne chose et j'ai commence cette habitude vers mes 15 ou 16 ans » , explique-t-il. Aujourd'hui, Moussa utilise son telephone pour signaler sa presence aux toilettes. « Je mettais mon telephone en musique et je rentrais avec pour signaler ma presence et aussi pour imiter mon grand-pere. J'y ai pris goût et jusqu'a present, je continue de le faire » , raconte-t-il. Pour lui, cette habitude ne pose pas vraiment de probleme : « En tout cas, ca ne me gene pas. » Un reflexe lie a notre rapport permanent au numerique Pour Sekou Doumbia, ingenieur en securite reseau a l'Agence des technologies de l'information et de la communication (AGTIC), cette pratique s'explique notamment par notre rapport de plus en plus constant au numerique. « L'utilisation du telephone aux toilettes s'explique principalement par notre incapacite moderne a tolerer l'ennui et le vide » , estime-t-il. Le smartphone permet ainsi de combler les quelques minutes passees aux toilettes. Une maniere de rester connecte, meme dans un moment qui etait autrefois davantage consacre a une simple pause. Une habitude qui agace ceux qui attendent Si certains apprecient ces minutes supplementaires avec leur telephone, ceux qui patientent a l'exterieur ont parfois un tout autre avis. « Ceux qui rentrent avec leur telephone dans les toilettes le font par conviction. Personnellement, je ne vois pas l'utilite. Et puis, ce n'est meme pas bien de parler dans les toilettes » , estime un homme d'environ une trentaine d'annees rencontre dans les rues de Bamako. Il dit preferer faire vite : « Je n'ai meme pas ce temps. Je fais mon besoin et je sors aussitot. » Meme son de cloche chez cet autre jeune rencontre sur place : « Tu ne peux pas prendre ton temps a manipuler ton telephone dans les toilettes alors qu'il y a des gens qui attendent dehors. Pour moi, ce n'est pas serieux. » Rester longtemps aux toilettes, quels risques pour la sante ? Au-dela de la gene occasionnee, rester longtemps assis aux toilettes peut egalement avoir des consequences sur la sante, selon le Dr Salaha Garba. « Rester assis longtemps dans les toilettes augmente la pression sur les veines de l'anus, ce qui peut favoriser les maladies hemorroïdaires » , explique-t-il. Selon le medecin, une position prolongee peut egalement favoriser une sensation de jambes lourdes. Le praticien recommande donc de ne pas prolonger inutilement le sejour aux toilettes. Selon lui, cinq a six minutes peuvent suffire dans la plupart des cas. Meme en cas de diarrhee, il conseille de sortir apres quelques minutes, de marcher un peu et de boire suffisamment d'eau avant de retourner aux toilettes si necessaire. Le smartphone peut donc accompagner cette pause, mais a condition de ne pas la transformer en longue seance de navigation. Quelques minutes peuvent rapidement devenir beaucoup plus longues lorsque le petit ecran capte toute l'attention. L’article Téléphone aux toilettes : quand le petit écran fait durer la pause est apparu en premier sur Studio Tamani - Informations, débats, magazines : toute l’actualité du Mali, en 5 langues .

items.title: Retour de New York : Mamadi Doumbouya accueilli par une forte mobilisation à Conakry
items.description: Après avoir pris part aux travaux de la 81ᵉ session ordinaire de l’Assemblée générale des Nations unies à New York, le président de la République, Mamadi Doumbouya, a regagné Conakry ce vendredi 25 septembre 2026. Son avion a atterri dans la matinée à l’aéroport international Ahmed-Sékou-Touré, au terme de plusieurs jours consacrés à une importante séquence diplomatique aux États-Unis. À son arrivée, le chef de l’État a été accueilli dans le cadre d’un cérémonial officiel auquel ont pris part plusieurs hautes personnalités de la République. Le Premier ministre, chef du gouvernement, les présidents des institutions républicaines, les membres du gouvernement, ainsi que des responsables civils et militaires figuraient parmi les personnalités présentes à l’aéroport. La cérémonie a également enregistré la présence de représentants des missions diplomatiques et consulaires accréditées en Guinée, ainsi que de responsables d’organisations internationales. Cette mobilisation avait été annoncée par le Cabinet civil de la Présidence, qui avait convié les autorités et personnalités concernées à prendre part au cérémonial d’accueil. Au-delà du dispositif officiel, une foule nombreuse s’est mobilisée aux abords de l’aéroport et le long de l’itinéraire présidentiel, brandissant notamment les couleurs nationales. Une importante présence citoyenne aux côtés des forces de sécurité chargées d’encadrer le dispositif. Ce retour intervient après la participation de Mamadi Doumbouya aux travaux de la 81ᵉ Assemblée générale de l’ONU, au cours desquels il a porté les positions et priorités de la Guinée sur la scène internationale. À New York, le chef de l’État a également eu des échanges avec plusieurs partenaires et a rencontré le secrétaire général des Nations unies, António Guterres. La séquence new-yorkaise désormais achevée, le président de la République retrouve ainsi Conakry, où son retour a été marqué par un important cérémonial républicain et une forte mobilisation populaire.

items.title: Discours contraires aux bonnes mœurs contre Victorine Ndèye : le procés de Désiré Pascal Maty renvoyé au 02 octobre
items.description: L’ancienne ministre de la Microfinance et de l’Économie sociale et solidaire, Victorine Anquediche Ndéye, s ’est désistée de sa constitution de partie civile et n’était pas devant la barre du tribunal des flagrants délits de Dakar ce vendredi, mais l’action publique se poursuit contre Désiré Pascal Maty. Ce dernier, âgé de 34 ans et agent dans le ministère qui a été dirigé par Mme Ndéye, est poursuivi pour des faits présumés de discours contraires aux bonnes mœurs, d’injures publiques, de menaces et de diffamation. L’affaire qui venait à la barre pour la première fois a été renvoyée au 2 octobre après que le tribunal a suivi le représentant du parquet qui s’est opposé à la demande de liberté provisoire formulée par la défense. Le représentant de la société a fait remarquer que n’importe qui aurait pu déposer une plainte vu la nature des propos tenus par le prévenu, dans les réseaux sociaux. A lire aussi : Offense au chef de l’Etat – discours contraires aux bonnes mœurs : peines fermes et amende pour Lamignou Darou et ses co-prévenus Interpellé par la Division spéciale de cybersécurité (Dsc), Désiré Pascal Maty, qui a été placé sous mandat de dépôt le 23 septembre, a fait une publication jugée discourtoise envers le maire de Niaguis. Cette dernière a déposé une plainte après avoir été alertée sur la sortie de Désiré Pascal Maty, par des proches. Au cours de l’enquête, le prévenu avait soutenu avoir réagi suite à des propos de Mme Ndéye. Hadja Diaw GAYE

items.title: Lawyer challenges Islamabad-Peshawar Motorway closure in IHC
items.description: ISLAMABAD: A lawyer moved the Islamabad High Court (IHC) on Friday against the closure of the Islamabad-Peshawar Motorway (M-1) and sought directions to reopen the blocked routes for lawyers, litigants and emergency services. The government announced the motorway’s closure earlier this week as it stepped up arrangements to prevent the PTI from marching on Islamabad. The march was part of the party’s planned nationwide protest to demand the release of its jailed founder, Imran Khan, and mobilise people for the supremacy of the Constitution. The protest was originally planned for Sept 27, but the party has now reportedly deferred it. Advocate Mian Shafqat Jan, a lawyer of the Supreme Court, filed a petition on Friday against the government’s move to shutdown the M-1 Motorway after he was unable to reach the Peshawar High Court (PHC) to appear in a case due to the closure. According to the petition, the lawyer was scheduled to appear before the PHC on Sept 24. He managed to enter the motorway from the Islamabad toll plaza at around 7am after facing difficulties but found the route closed at the M-1 Attock Bridge. The petitioner said he sought information from officials deployed at the site about any written order authorising the closure but was unable to obtain a confirmation. He contended that closing public routes without a notification, written order or disclosed reasons infringed citizens’ fundamental rights and warranted judicial intervention. The petition named the federation through the interior and information secretaries, the inspectors general of the National Highways and Motorway Police and Islamabad Police, the National Highway Authority through its chairman, the Islamabad Capital Territory administration through the chief commissioner, and the Punjab government through its home secretary and inspector general of police as respondents. The petitioner also referred to a recent IHC judgement about the planned PTI protest, arguing that the court had recognised constitutional protections for citizens, including freedom of movement and access to courts. In its detailed 37-page judgement in the case pertaining to the PTI’s planned protest, the IHC held that any activity resulting in the infringement of citizens’ fundamental rights amounted to a violation of the Constitution. It also observed that the right to peaceful assembly could not be exercised in a manner that infringed the rights of other citizens. The bench, headed by Chief Justice Sardar Muhammad Sarfraz Dogar and comprising Justice Muhammad Azam Khan and Justice Muhammad Asif, directed the authorities to ensure that no political party, leader or public office holder occupied roads, highways, interchanges or toll plazas in a manner that obstructed free movement or hindered access to medical and educational facilities. On the basis of these arguments, Advocate Jan urged the high court in his plea to declare the closure of roads and highways without any notification, written order or disclosed reasons illegal and unconstitutional. He has also sought directions for the interior secretary, communications secretary and Islamabad chief commissioner to ensure the reopening of blocked routes for emergency traffic, lawyers, litigants, witnesses, sick persons, funeral processions and other emergency services. According to the National Highways and Motorway Police (NHMP), the M-1 has been closed to all traffic in both directions between the Islamabad Toll Plaza and Chhachh Interchange, while the M-14 was closed from Hakla to Kundal. The GT Road was also closed at Attock Khurd. The government had also decided to close the Islamabad-Dera Ismail Khan Motorway (M14) — also known as the CPEC road — and GT Road. Security arrangements were also intensified in Attock, with containers and sandbags placed at key bridges and security tightened at major entry and exit points, as authorities prepared for the PTI protest. The federal government also approved the deployment of Rangers in Islamabad and several districts of Punjab ahead of the PTI’s planned march on the federal capital. Punjab has already imposed a ban on gatherings across the province for 13 days and prohibited inciting people to “unlawful assembly”. A similar ban under Section 144 has been enforced in Islamabad as well for two months. Gatherings in the federal capital are also banned under the Peaceful Assembly and Public Order Act 2024 , which had been rushed through the National Assembly amidst the opposition’s outcry ahead of a PTI gathering . Meanwhile, Section 144 has also been imposed in Karachi, Hyderabad, Sukkur and Balochistan. The Punjab government had also sent a letter to the federal interior ministry requesting mobile and internet services at specific locations in Rawalpindi and Attock to be downgraded or jammed on Sept 27 due to the “expected law and order situation”.

items.title: 140 armes saisies chez un homme d’affaires
items.description: La police sud-africaine a annoncé, le jeudi 24 septembre 2026, l’arrestation d’un homme d’affaires de 60 ans à Mthatha, dans la province du Cap-Oriental. Une opération de contrôle menée au siège de sa société de sécurité a permis de saisir 140 armes à feu, alors que 135 autres restent introuvables. Le suspect était déjà en liberté sous caution dans une affaire de tentative de meurtre visant un policier. L’homme d’affaires est désormais confronté à de nouvelles poursuites pour violation présumée de la législation sud-africaine sur le contrôle des armes à feu. Son interpellation est intervenue à la suite d’une inspection de conformité conduite cette semaine à Mthatha par des éléments de la police sud-africaine (SAPS), dans le cadre de l’«Operation Buyisa». Selon la SAPS, les enquêteurs ont découvert que le sexagénaire détenait une arme appartenant à sa société sans disposer du permis requis, en violation présumée de l’article 3(1)(a) de la Firearms Control Act 60 of 2000. Les vérifications ont également fait ressortir des irrégularités dans la gestion de l’arsenal de la société de sécurité. Plusieurs armes enregistrées au nom de l’entreprise ne figuraient pas dans son registre des stocks. Au total, 140 armes à feu ont été saisies, tandis que 135 autres demeurent introuvables, précise la police. L’affaire prend une dimension supplémentaire puisque le suspect était déjà en liberté sous caution dans un autre dossier. Il est poursuivi pour tentative de meurtre après un incident survenu en juillet 2026, au cours duquel un policier qui n’était pas en service avait été blessé par balle. D’après les éléments communiqués par la police, l’homme d’affaires aurait tiré à l’intérieur d’une tente lors d’une cérémonie traditionnelle, atteignant le policier. Cette affaire est toujours pendante devant la justice. Pour son nouveau dossier lié à la détention présumée illégale d’armes, le suspect doit comparaître le mardi 29 septembre 2026 devant le tribunal de première instance de Mthatha, notamment dans le cadre de la procédure relative à sa mise en liberté sous caution. Les 140 armes récupérées seront soumises à des expertises balistiques. Les enquêteurs chercheront notamment à déterminer si certaines d’entre elles ont pu servir dans la commission d’autres crimes graves ou violents. La SAPS assure, pour sa part, que les opérations de contrôle se poursuivront auprès des détenteurs d’armes et des entreprises concernées, avec pour objectif de faire respecter la législation et de limiter la circulation ainsi que l’utilisation illégale des armes à feu. Par Valentin SOMANDE L’article 140 armes saisies chez un homme d’affaires est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: Retour à Conakry : Mamadi Doumbouya au contact de la foule après son arrivée
items.description: Le Président de la République, Mamadi Doumbouya, est arrivé à Conakry ce vendredi 25 septembre 2026, après sa participation à la 81ᵉ session de l’Assemblée générale des Nations Unies à New York. Après l’incident survenu le 23 dernier à New York, selon plusieurs témoignages sur les lieux:«c’est une façon pour nous de montrer que le peuple guinéen est derrière lui». Annoncé à 09h, la mobilisation a débuté au alentours de 7h. L’avion présidentiel a atterri à 11h57 à l’aéroport international Ahmed Sékou Touré de Conakry. À 12h09, le chef de l’État est apparu au contact de la foule mobilisée pour l’accueillir. Face aux personnes présentes, Mamadi Doumbouya a d’abord posé sa main en direction de la foule, avant de lui adresser un bisou. Ce geste intervient après une précédente réception au cours de laquelle le chef de l’État était resté à bord de son véhicule de commandement. Pour ce retour au pays, le Président de la République arborait exceptionnellement un boubou blanc brodé aux couleurs du tricolore guinéen, accompagné d’un chapeau traditionnel. Après son passage au contact de la foule, Mamadi Doumbouya a pris place à bord d’une Toyota noire. Il a ensuite quitté l’aéroport, entouré de véhicules équipés de gyrophares de proximité et accompagné de son cortège habituel, en direction de Kaloum, le centre-ville de Conakry. Sur l’itinéraire, notamment à partir de Gbessia Kondébounyi, des mobilisations étaient perceptibles. Des citoyens s’étaient rassemblés le long de la route pour saluer le passage du cortège présidentiel. Le retour du chef de l’État intervient au lendemain de plusieurs appels à la mobilisation lancés à Conakry pour accueillir son retour de New York. Mayi Cissé L’article Retour à Conakry : Mamadi Doumbouya au contact de la foule après son arrivée est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: How to Destroy a Lesbian Bar
items.description: Way back in the wilds of 2013, I organized an event on feminism at a public venue in London. I was then the online editor of a left-wing magazine, and we had some of the best feminist columnists around. What a chance to show them off! A warm and supportive evening to celebrate a social movement that was then having a resurgence! Can you guess where this is going?! I remembered that event as I read The Boston Globe ’s extraordinarily viral account this week of a meltdown at the Last Ditch Bar and Arts Venue in Greenfield, Massachusetts. The lesbian bar strayed from the path of righteousness—brace yourselves—by announcing late last month that it would go mask-optional on Saturday nights. (“Greenfield hasn’t reported any COVID cases in more than two months,” the Globe ’s Annalisa Quinn notes.) The bar was deluged with complaints that it was engaged in a “mass disabling event” that would kill its patrons, and was “no better than a fascist.” Even worse, some people involved were probably white women. One Instagram user, an artist who goes by Soe Noire, accused the owners of flirting with eugenics and “putting profit over people.” Now, my event didn’t quite generate that level of take-me-to-the-fainting-couch backlash. But we were besieged online by a squadron of nitpickers, who started from the position that they hated the event and worked backwards to find out why. Deviously, I had foiled them by ensuring that the panel was racially mixed, and by including a transgender woman, foreclosing the promising “cis white bitches” line of attack then popular in feminist circles. The hall was wheelchair-accessible and had a hearing loop for deaf attendees, Gaza had not yet emerged as a purity test, and COVID was not even a twinkle in a diseased bat’s eye. Conceding that the event had passed every intersectional test, the detractors fell back on the great constant: capitalism. Although all of the panelists had waived their speaking fee, we were charging £5 (about $6.50) a ticket, to cover the room rental. Was I not aware, one tweeter asked, that £5 was the cost of a meal to a single mother? Checkmate. The crime had been found, and I was guilty of being a privileged idiot, rolling around in my feminist loot like Scrooge McDuck. [ Thomas Chatterton Williams: The left’s new moralism will backfire ] The event went ahead, but you never knew when one person’s gripe would derail everything; what we had envisioned as a warm, community-focused discussion instead felt like volunteering for a sprint through a minefield. (In the end, none of the haters turned up, and it was a pleasant evening.) This was the moment when I realized that social media had empowered drive-by whinings by sociopaths, and that progressive politics had allowed them to cloak themselves in righteousness. What might once have been recognized as narcissism, jealousy, the result of a personality disorder—or just plain boredom—was now transfigured into “calling out” those who had erred. The people pointing fingers usually did nothing themselves, apart from complaining, which had the happy side effect that they could never be accused of committing an impure act. My experience pales beside that of Jackie Matellian, the 26-year-old proprietor of the Last Ditch, who, according to the Globe , had run up $50,000 in debt and had been sleeping in her truck as a result of the business’s troubles. She tried to do everything right: The bar was declared to be a safe space for the unhoused, and a no-go zone for police. She and her former co-owners (one of whom uses it/its pronouns) waived the cover charge for anyone who couldn’t pay; more and more patrons took advantage. After the backlash to the change in the mask policy, the bar apologized , explaining that the mask-optional night would help members of the queer community who needed to lip-read. None of this appeased the critics, one of whom felt the bar was insufficiently devoted to “revolutionary praxis,” which is like normal praxis but the discussions you have about it go around and around forever. “How are we supposed to be ‘connected in the revolution’ if we are spreading disease to one another? Nah,” Soe Noire posted . At this point, Matellian should have realized that you can’t negotiate with terrorists, even ones with long COVID. Instead, though, she optimistically subjected herself to a struggle session—sorry, a mediation-and-accountability process—so that everyone could air their grievances. The podcast Blocked and Reported , which broke the story of the Last Ditch earlier this month, obtained audio recordings of this meeting, in which pronoun declarations were required. As Katie Herzog, a co-host of the podcast, observed, the participants included “two people named after plants” (Sage and Moss; a third was named Yams). Those attending on Zoom were relentlessly hostile, demanding to know the mediator’s race and whether they would be institutionalized for disclosing any mental-health conditions to her. One of the Last Ditch volunteers told the meeting that the bar was $3,900 in debt and needed to pay within days, but Soe Noire—a self-declared lesbian using he/him pronouns—changed the subject to how the policy change made him feel unsafe. The Last Ditch had failed to uphold “COVID-cautious principles, anti-racism, or revolution,” Noire said. (Reminder: This is a bar. You know, the place where you go to drink beer.) Most people might be surprised that arguments over masking are still so febrile years after even cautious blue-state schools resumed in-person teaching. But across the United States, some small subcultures live as though it’s still April 2020. That’s because pandemic protections and mitigations quickly became left-coded, to the extent that Donald Trump now has to pretend he didn’t oversee the successful vaccine program. In this context, perma-masking is every bit as much a political symbol as wearing a MAGA hat or a keffiyeh. Anxiety and depression rates spiked during the pandemic, and some vulnerable people have never really recovered from the effects of physical isolation and the sense of oppressive dread they felt during months when thousands of Americans died. On the right, these emotions drive people toward conspiracism about Chinese bioweapons and false flags and “mass formation psychosis,” the idea that gullible populations were hypnotized into accepting shutdown measures. On the left, these anxieties coincide with a political critique—that Americans and their predatory private-health-care system do not care about disabled people. Masking is a visible symbol of resistance to this injustice, as well as a practical measure against the spread of disease. Notably, too, self-reported long COVID is disproportionately high among trans and bi Americans. Unless science uncovers measurable respiratory differences between bisexuals and the rest of the population, one explanation is that more LGBTQ Americans live in social contexts in which vague, unpleasant symptoms such as brain fog are interpreted as long COVID. The political division helps explain why masking is portrayed in certain progressive enclaves as a way of resisting eugenics. But it doesn’t quite explain the boiling fury of the people demanding masks at the Last Ditch. At this point, let me also bring in the word mimophant . This is a term for someone who has the hide of an elephant when criticizing others, but the delicate skin of a mimosa flower when criticized themselves. At the mediation meeting, Soe Noire, who had previously performed at the bar but was otherwise not deeply involved with it, was extremely attentive to his own feelings of pain. He also groused that while other speakers were limited to two minutes apiece, Matellian—who had faced sniping from all sides for more than an hour—chose to “go overtime and cry for three minutes.” Anyone who has spent time in dysfunctional activist spaces will be familiar with this dynamic: The designated target is expected to soak up endless criticism in silence, or even express gratitude for the correction. If the target gets upset, they can be accused of “centering their own pain” at the expense of the marginalized. Robin DiAngelo’s best-selling White Fragility has a whole section about the tendency of certain women to weep in such circumstances, a phenomenon she dismisses as “white tears.” The overall effect of this approach is like when a school bully slams someone into the lockers and then taunts them for crying. Oh, the widdle baby got hurt, did they? This is sadism disguised as activism. The audio reveals that Noire followed up on his complaint by explaining that “as a trans person, there’s a lot of emotional and physical labor that goes into this.” (The physical labor of—whining?) Returning for another meeting would expose Noire to “harm.” In the second round of complaints, Noire demanded a complete change of leadership in the bar’s management team, and concluded: “Pay me.” What followed my own feminist-event drama was a political education. Gradually, my friendship group began to pass around articles that made sense of the patterns we were seeing. In a 2012 blog post, the writer Matt Bruenig described what he called “purity leftism.” “When purity leftists do actions and organizing, their interest is not in reducing oppression as much as it is in reducing their own participation in it,” he wrote . “Above all else, they want to be able to say that they are not oppressing, not that oppression has ended.” Such people were prone, Bruenig said, to “self-marginalizing lifestyles and costumes.” A year later, he offered another useful phrase: identitarian deference , or the presumption that “privileged individuals should defer to the opinions and views of oppressed individuals.” Since then, I have become alert to all of the red flags of purity leftism: complaints about “white tears,” the sadism of the get-up-so-I-can-hit-you-again tendency, the use of jargon such as praxis while fretting that the conversation is dominated by the privileged, and the hyperbolic assertions of nebulous “harm.” (Rhetorical inflation has gotten so bad that everything is a genocide.) [ Helen Lewis: The Gaza left and the gender left ] These gambits work because accommodating the oppressed and less fortunate is a social good. Public venues should have wheelchair ramps, and you shouldn’t go to the children’s cancer ward with a terrible head cold. What the purity leftists exploit is a reluctance to say how much accommodation is enough. If masking was desirable at the height of the COVID pandemic, it must still be appropriate now—and anyone who says otherwise doesn’t care about the disabled. If respecting people with gender dysphoria is a sign of tolerance, then no one should question whether calling a human being “it” is reasonable or progressive. Communities that talk like this are very attached to the concept of “mutual aid,” but some people suck up a lot of care and support without ever putting a shift in to help others. Good-natured herbivorous lefties are easy marks for narcissists and mimophants. It’s noteworthy that the Last Ditch meltdown was caused, ultimately, by the pandemic of 2020. The coronavirus and wokeness were two novel pathogens. Our physical immune system didn’t know how to react to COVID, while our social immune system adapted slowly to the speed with which activists organized on social media. Several of the cancellations I covered in that period would not have played out the same way without Slack groups, Zoom meetings, and Twitter threads—forums that allowed bad actors to dominate the discussion, and prevented the broad mass of reasonable people from realizing that they were in the majority. I’ve lost count of the number of times a small clique of whiners so hijacked a left-wing event that the organizers eventually conceded defeat: One fond memory is of the fat-positive club that was forced to apologize for playing the song “Spice Up Your Life” because one of the lyrics refers to a “yellow man in Timbuktu.” The situation at the Last Ditch is very similar. Soe Noire rampaged through Greenfield’s LGBTQ community like a dose of the clap. The most interesting aspect of the Last Ditch saga has been the reaction. The story drove 1,000 subscriptions to the Globe , and generated more traffic than any other article the paper had published this year, according to Semafor ’s Max Tani. Even on Bluesky, the spiritual home of perma-masking, the response settled somewhere around “the pandemic broke people’s brains,” with the occasional interjection that queer communities should not air their grievances in public, for the sake of the movement. Soe Noire alone is unrepentant, posting on Instagram that “the antimaskers and randos coming in to give their useless two cents, you might wanna read a book.” In the 13 years since I got mobbed for charging £5 to attend an event, and the six years since the beginning of the pandemic, our social immune system has learned to adapt. Even the 83-year-old Democratic ranking member of the House Appropriations Committee, Rosa DeLauro, has been joking online about taking a tour group to the bar. The Last Ditch’s future might be precarious, but so is the future of the social-justice protection racket.

items.title: Maybe Alex Gibney Did Elon Musk a Favor
items.description: Watching Musk can feel a bit like staring into the sun—uncomfortable and unpleasant, given that the new documentary is almost four hours long and is filled with distressing footage of the richest man in the world. Despite Elon Musk being a near-permanent fixture in the headlines, the film pushes viewers to pay even closer attention to him, arguing that Musk’s motivations for amassing so much power are as important to scrutinize as how he did so. Maybe the mogul truly seeks to establish a future in which people walk on Mars. Or maybe, the director Alex Gibney posits, Musk has built his influence over millions of electric-vehicle customers, social-media users, and Donald Trump supporters so that he can shape this world as he sees fit. Musk, unsurprisingly, isn’t pleased with the film. In a series of posts on X, Musk called the project a “hit piece” and Gibney a “horrible human.” In a letter to Gibney’s company, Jigsaw Productions, Musk’s lawyer Alex Spiro threatened to file a defamation lawsuit. Spiro took issue in particular with the documentary’s suggestion that Musk may be able to use the Starlink satellites owned by his rocket company, SpaceX, to influence elections. (Jigsaw said in a statement that the First Amendment protects its “right to engage in open debate and fact-based examinations of powerful public figures.”) When we spoke ahead of Musk ’s North American premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival earlier this month, Gibney didn’t sound fazed. The Oscar-winning documentarian has dealt with intimidating legal battles before; for his 2015 film Going Clear , which examined the notoriously litigious Church of Scientology, an HBO executive at the time joked that the network had hired some 160 lawyers to withstand the organization’s potential response. For Musk , Gibney recruited independent fact-checkers to audit his team’s research, stress-testing the material presented on-screen more thoroughly than anything else in his filmography. “It’s never good for the lawyer for the richest man in the world to threaten to sue you,” Gibney told me. “But we’ve prepared for it by being really rigorous and being true to the facts.” [ Read: Elon Musk is playing God ] Still, the troubles surrounding Musk have only grown. Shortly after I spoke with Gibney, The Hollywood Reporter detailed the possibility that the film would not be distributed abroad after its theatrical U.S. debut, on October 9. Universal, the studio handling the documentary’s international rights, reportedly considered the project “politically sensitive for parts of the Trump administration” and contemplated not distributing it at all. (Per Variety , however, Musk will be released abroad as planned; though the publication cited “sources familiar with the project,” Universal did not comment on the rollout.) If the film fails to secure a release beyond its North American date, the move would be in line with how Gibney described Musk’s ethos to me. “He has gone to enormous lengths and expense, including buying the presidency of the United States, in order to be able to manufacture a narrative that suits him,” Gibney said of the businessman. “He doesn’t like it when that narrative is upended.” Musk refused to be interviewed for Gibney’s documentary, but the director had a plan in mind. In previous documentaries such as Client 9 , about the Eliot Spitzer prostitution scandal, and Zero Days , a dive into the computer virus Stuxnet, the filmmaker deployed actors as stand-ins for subjects who couldn’t appear on camera. For the former, he sought to protect a vulnerable source’s privacy; for the latter, the NSA whistleblowers he spoke with would have been prosecuted for their participation. But as Gibney and his team sifted through footage of Musk’s previous interviews, they decided to go further: They turned him into a digital creation, inspired by how often he spoke about reality being a simulation. “We thought, Well, fuck it, let’s do that with Elon ,” he recalled. Using AI tools to help sync the fake Musk’s facial movements with the real Musk’s voice, Gibney sought to underline the “contradictions of the technology itself.” The decision has led to some confusion. Halfway through my screening of Musk , during the intermission, a publicist for the film clarified that the digital representation of Musk that recited things the real Musk had said wasn’t AI-generated, as some reviews of the film following its premiere at the Venice International Film Festival had claimed. He’s computer -generated, the publicist said, and therefore created by humans. In those critics’ defense, it’s hard to tell. Visually, the animated Musk—dubbed the “Avatar” by Gibney and the designers at the visual-effects studio MakeMake—exists in the uncanny valley of video-game characters and AI-generated deepfakes. His eyes, staring directly into the camera, look soulless. His movements are strangely fluid. He’s more chiseled than the real Musk—“I think I did him a favor,” Gibney said—and he appears to be seated inside a spaceship. To the director, the more jarring the Avatar looked amid an otherwise-serious film, the better. “I’m playing in Elon’s sandbox,” Gibney said, citing Musk’s penchant for posting eye-searing memes. “I mean, this is a guy who traffics in poop emojis online.” Speaking Musk’s language, though, might not protect the film from more of his ire. Gibney said that he’s concerned about whether Musk will reach wider audiences in time to avoid the forthcoming mega-merger between Paramount and Warner Brothers Discovery, which owns HBO; the network is set to air the project sometime in 2027, before it eventually streams on HBO Max. “I’m not sure I trust David Ellison and/or Larry Ellison to be as supportive,” he said, referring to the possibility that the Paramount CEO and his billionaire father, both of whom have close ties with Musk, may not be inclined to back the film as much as HBO has thus far. (To further complicate matters, Semafor also reported this week that Paramount is considering asking Musk to become an investor to help the company absorb Warner Bros. Discovery.) The film is certainly stuffed with material that, to my mind, could cause Musk’s allies to bristle at it reaching as many viewers as possible: Apart from the theory about Starlink satellites swaying elections, the documentary also raises questions about how DOGE’s access to millions of Americans’ personal data could violate individual freedoms, a concern that emerged even before DOGE achieved “ God mode ,” as my colleagues Ian Bogost and Charlie Warzel reported. There are sections that look closely at Musk’s personal life as well, including his alleged betrayals of his former business partners at Tesla and his seeming obsession with having children with as many women as possible—so far 14 children with four women. (Musk settled a lawsuit filed by Tesla’s first CEO, Martin Eberhard, in 2009 that allowed Musk to be called a co-founder of the company.) [ Read: The decline and fall of Elon Musk ] Yet for everything that he gets to in Musk , Gibney said that he also left plenty out so the film wouldn’t balloon past its already-colossal runtime. He’d wanted to include more about how Musk’s bullish investment in AI makes the stock market more volatile, potentially damaging people's retirement funds down the line if the AI bubble bursts. He’d hoped to explore an angle on Silicon Valley’s ties to Russia. He had a “great whistleblower” on the story of SolarCity, a company founded by Musk’s cousins that was later absorbed by Tesla. But what he’s ultimately missing, of course, is Musk himself. In the documentary, Gibney illustrates that his subject is worth intense analysis in part because it has become almost impossible to penetrate the muck that orbits the mogul—the paper trails of litigation, the rabbit holes of conspiracy theories, the fiery social-media exchanges. “In an interview, you want to be able to create a circumstance where someone is going to be reflective and considered and searching for deeper meaning,” Gibney explained. “I'm not sure Elon is in a place now where he does anything more than put a moat around himself.” To the filmmaker, Musk is merely the man behind the curtain, presenting an “Oz-like image”—an image that involves regularly calling himself a champion of free speech. If Musk truly means what he says, then he should be fine with a documentary interrogating his actions reaching as many viewers as possible.

items.title: An Underappreciated Problem With Dating Apps
items.description: Many modern daters seem to have the same complaint: water, water everywhere, but not a drop to drink. Possible mates abound—on dating apps, in the databases of professional matchmakers—but none of them appeal. As one woman quoted in a recent New York magazine article put it, “The odds are good, but the goods are odd.” Another article , in The New York Times, featured a 38-year-old man who had been on 40 first dates but had yet to find a keeper. He said that he’d gone out with one woman who’d seemed good “on paper” but that he’d nevertheless felt that “there was something that was … off.” My colleague Faith Hill has reported that more and more Americans are having a hard time finding love, no matter which app they’re on or which service they’re using. Researchers have offered various explanations for this problem, but an underappreciated one, several academics told me, is that people don’t hang out as much as they once did in mixed-gender, non-dating contexts. The modern form of dating, in which two strangers who were set up by a matchmaker or an algorithm sit down at a restaurant, conduct 90 minutes of small talk, and try to determine if there’s a “spark,” is not a very good way to find love. [ Read: Too scared for sex ] For much of American history, most people met their partner through family, friends, church, or—as coed universities and offices became more common—college and work. They got to know each other before becoming romantic. “You hung out with folks, and sometimes the sparks started to grow slowly from that,” the UC Davis psychology professor Paul Eastwick told me. In 1970, for example , about a third of heterosexual couples met through friends, but by 2020, the number was 20 percent. The percentage of people who met through family, school, college, or work also fell during that period. When people become acquainted through social or professional networks, they can get to know each other gradually, through casual, repeated socializing. This allows inside jokes to bloom and first impressions to correct themselves—or not. Most people are more of an acquired taste than an immediate yes. After chatting informally four or five times in the dining hall or break room, some people will realize that they don’t care for each other at all, but others will like each other much more than they did initially. Opportunities for these kinds of interactions have become more limited. Americans today spend much less time with friends than they did 20 years ago, and many people—young men in particular —have few or no friends of the opposite sex. Starting a relationship with a co-worker has also become thornier in recent years as awareness of sexual harassment and unhealthy power dynamics has grown. When people pay for apps or matchmaking services, meanwhile, they may approach dates thinking, “I should be able to find exactly what I’m looking for,” Liesel Sharabi, a communication professor at Arizona State University who has studied dating, told me. She said that this is “the wrong attitude to have.” Instead of assuming that the perfect partner is out there waiting to be found, daters should try to understand that people generally build compatibility over time . They should aim for the mindset that “I’m gonna make something work with somebody,” and “I’m going to build the type of relationship I want,” Sharabi said. In a recent study , she and two colleagues followed hundreds of dating-app users for three months. Many of the daters said that they experienced “emotional exhaustion and inefficacy.” Sharabi said that their burnout was caused in part by the sheer number of possible matches that her subjects were scrolling through, and the fact that dating had started to feel an awful lot like a part-time job. [ Read: Most people don’t have a ‘type’ ] Another reason people have trouble finding partners they like is that apps and matchmaking services allow people to screen for qualities such as height, education, and age. But these are shallow criteria, Sharabi and others say, and they do not actually help people predict who they will like as a long-term partner. If someone is two inches shorter than your preferred height, Sharabi said, “six months into a relationship, other qualities usually matter a lot more.” Pamela Torres, the founder of the Offline Social, an Austin-based company that organizes events for single people including golf and pickleball, told me that “chemistry happens when you meet someone and then you make an exception” to your usual dating checklist. Group settings can also reveal more about a person than a one-on-one first date. A potential mate’s humor under pressure, or kindness toward others, may be on display during a volunteer activity but can be harder to pick up on when they’re auditioning for the role of boyfriend. “What really counts in a relationship developing into love is how that person interacts with other people as well as you , ” Stephanie Coontz, an emeritus family-studies professor at Evergreen State College and the author of For Better and Worse , told me. Coontz met her husband when they worked together on political projects. “I didn’t even think of him as attractive,” she said, “the first two or three times I met him, until suddenly he seemed very handsome to me.” Eastwick and others say that people struggling with dating could consider focusing less energy on optimizing their app profiles and more on socializing in groups. For instance: Join a hiking club; throw parties ; flirt—in a respectful and non-harassy way!—with your co-worker ; and otherwise engage in activities you enjoy, and see whether someone else who enjoys doing them might be a good partner. Any given outing or interaction may not instantly produce Mr. Right. Torres said that her organization doesn’t promise to help people “find the love of your life in one night” but rather to simply “take people out of their houses.” People may not find their soulmate at the first hole of golf, but by the back nine, they may at least have found someone they’d like to see again.

items.title: 'Tremendous things will be happening': Trump hails 'very productive' meeting with China's Xi
items.description: US President Donald Trump on Friday concluded his “productive” meeting with Chinese President XI Jinping, noting in a post on Truth Social that “tremendous things will be happening”. “Like almost everyone else, he seemed to like calling the poorly and inaccurately named artificial intelligence to a far more accurate and important name: super intelligence. That would be ‘super!’ Everyone last night agreed, also,” he wrote. The lavish state summit at the White House appeared heavy on symbolism but light on substance, with no sign of major breakthroughs between the world’s biggest economies. Still, Trump highlighted progress under a bilateral trade mechanism , citing what he described as increased market access for US farmers and ranchers, while both leaders identified artificial intelligence as an area for cooperation. Trump would follow up his summit with Xi by taking the Chinese leader to the US National Archives, where they were expected to stress views about the history and direction of ties between their countries. A newspaper featuring a front page photo of China’s President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump, at a White House welcome ceremony, is seen at a news stand in Beijing on September 25, 2026. —AFP Trump said in remarks welcoming Xi that they would see some of the greatest treasures of US history at the National Archives, including the Declaration of Independence, the US Constitution and the Bill of Rights. They would also see “artifacts testifying to the long and cherished relationship” between China and the United States and their “cultural exchanges”, he said. “Just as our ancestors reached across the ocean centuries ago to trade, to learn, and to build a better world, our two countries do really the same thing, and we’re very proud of it and the relationship,” Trump said. China has not commented on the visit to the archives, but analysts say Xi may be keen to see records relating to the US switch of recognition to communist China from Taiwan in 1979. China presses on Taiwan Xi has long sought to persuade Trump to state publicly that the United States opposes Taiwan’s independence , rather than saying only that it does not support independence, which has been Washington’s formulation for decades. He is also keen to get the US to halt arms sales to the island. As expected, Xi pressed Trump on Taiwan on Thursday, saying he hoped the United States would “handle the Taiwan question with prudence.” China’s state news agency also reported that Xi “hopes the US side will adhere to the correct position of opposing ‘Taiwan independence’.” While the United States, like most countries, has no formal diplomatic relations with Taipei, Washington is its most important international backer and is bound by US law to provide it with the means to defend itself. America’s Asian allies will watch closely to see how Trump talks about Taiwan following Xi’s visit. After his May summit with Xi, Trump, whose administration in December approved an $11 billion arms sale package to Taiwan, said he was holding a second package, worth some $14bn, in abeyance and described it as a “very good negotiating chip.” Craig Singleton of the Foundation for Defence of Democracies think tank said Beijing may believe it has established a new baseline on Taiwan with Trump. (L-R) China’s First Lady Peng Liyuan, China’s President Xi Jinping, US President Donald Trump and US First Lady Melania Trump look on during a military review in the Rose Garden of the White House in Washington, DC, on September 24, 2026. —AFP He said Xi’s use of the word “adhere” was revealing because “it implies Beijing believes Washington is already behaving in ways it wants.” “In the context of the current stand-down on Taiwan arms sales, China may increasingly view that restraint as a new baseline rather than a temporary pause,” he said. “Beijing’s objective is to get Trump to absorb Chinese red lines into his own definition of a stable relationship.” On Thursday, Senate Democrats criticised the summit, saying Trump had failed to secure meaningful concessions from Beijing on trade, security, artificial intelligence or human rights. They also criticised Trump for failing to publicly address China’s military pressure on Taiwan and called for the immediate delivery of approved military aid and arms sales to the island.

items.title: Athlétisme : 38 ans après l’argent de Dia Bâ, Saly Sarr, nouvel espoir olympique du Sénégal
items.description: Le 25 septembre 1988, à Séoul, El Hadji Amadou Dia Bâ offrait au Sénégal la première et, à ce jour, l’unique médaille olympique de son histoire. Trente-huit ans après cet exploit, le pays attend toujours un nouvel héritier. Entre les sacres mondiaux d’Amy Mbacké Thiam et l’ascension fulgurante de Saly Sarr, l’espoir d’un nouveau podium olympique semble toutefois se dessiner. Il est des exploits dont le temps n’altère ni l’éclat ni la portée. Celui réalisé par El Hadji Amadou Dia Bâ, le 25 septembre 1988 au stade olympique de Séoul, appartient à cette catégorie. À 30 ans, le spécialiste du 400 m haies entrait dans l’histoire du sport sénégalais en décrochant la médaille d’argent des Jeux olympiques, offrant au Sénégal sa toute première distinction olympique. Dans une finale d’exception, le pensionnaire de l’US Gorée bouclait les 400 m haies en 47 s 23, à seulement quatre centièmes de l’Américain André Phillips, médaillé d’or en 47 s 19. Il devançait notamment une légende de la discipline, Edwin Moses, troisième en 47 s 56. Près de quatre décennies plus tard, cette performance demeure une référence majeure de l’athlétisme sénégalais. Ce jour-là, Dia Bâ n’avait pas seulement remporté une médaille. Il avait ouvert une brèche et démontré qu’un athlète sénégalais pouvait rivaliser avec l’élite mondiale. À la veille de la finale, le juge Kéba Mbaye lui aurait lancé : « Demain, tu ne cours pas pour toi. Tu cours pour 6 millions de Sénégalais. » Une phrase devenue emblématique dans le récit de cet exploit. Atlanta 1996 : le relais sénégalais au pied du podium Après l’argent de Dia Bâ à Séoul, le relais sénégalais a été le plus proche d’un nouveau podium olympique. Aux Jeux d’Atlanta, en 1996, l’équipe du 4 × 400 m, composée d’Ibou Faye, Moustapha Diarra, Aboubakry Dia et Hachim Ndiaye, terminait à la quatrième place de la finale, en 3 min 00 s 64. Une performance qui reste, à ce jour, le record national. Les quatre sprinteurs échouaient ainsi au pied du podium, à quelques centièmes de la médaille de bronze. Une nouvelle occasion manquée pour le Sénégal de prolonger la trace laissée huit ans plus tôt par Dia Bâ. Amy Mbacké Thiam, l’or mondial sans médaille olympique Au fil des années, d’autres grandes figures ont porté haut les couleurs du Sénégal sur la scène internationale, sans parvenir à monter sur un podium olympique. Amy Mbacké Thiam demeure l’une des plus illustres. En 2001, à Edmonton, au Canada, elle devenait championne du monde du 400 m. Deux ans plus tard, aux Mondiaux de Paris, elle confirmait son statut parmi les meilleures spécialistes de la discipline en décrochant la médaille de bronze. Son palmarès aurait pu s’enrichir d’une distinction olympique. Mais aux Jeux d’Athènes, en 2004, la championne sénégalaise ne parvenait pas à franchir le cap des demi-finales du 400 m. Son parcours résume, à lui seul, le paradoxe de l’athlétisme sénégalais depuis Séoul : des performances de premier plan sur la scène mondiale, mais aucun nouveau podium aux Jeux. Saly Sarr, l’espoir d’un nouveau rêve olympique Aujourd’hui, un nouveau nom concentre les espoirs : Saly Sarr. À 23 ans, la spécialiste du triple saut s’est progressivement installée parmi les références internationales de sa discipline et multiplie les performances de haut niveau. Le 23 août 2026, lors de la Diamond League de Silésie, en Pologne, la Sénégalaise réalisait un bond de 15,08 m, établissant un nouveau record national. Elle effaçait ainsi des tablettes l’ancienne marque de 15,00 m détenue par la regrettée Kène Ndoye. Quelques jours plus tard, le 4 septembre, Saly Sarr franchissait un nouveau cap en remportant la finale de la Diamond League à Bruxelles, avec un saut à 14,96 m. Elle devenait ainsi la première athlète sénégalaise à s’adjuger le prestigieux circuit. Le 13 septembre, elle confirmait encore sa montée en puissance en remportant le concours du triple saut du World Athletics Ultimate Championship, à Budapest, avec une performance de 15,06 m. Ces résultats témoignent d’une progression spectaculaire. Championne d’Afrique, médaillée mondiale en salle et désormais victorieuse dans les plus grandes compétitions internationales, Saly Sarr accumule les références qui nourrissent les ambitions sénégalaises. Los Angeles 2028 en ligne de mire Saly Sarr entend désormais écrire une nouvelle page de l’histoire du triple saut sénégalais, dans le sillage de Kène Ndoye. Spécialiste du triple saut et du saut en longueur, cette dernière avait atteint la finale des Jeux olympiques d’Athènes en 2004, où elle avait terminé à la 14ᵉ place. Elle avait auparavant décroché le bronze aux Mondiaux en salle de 2003. À Paris, en 2024, Saly Sarr n’était pas parvenue à se qualifier pour la finale du triple saut. Deux ans plus tard, ses performances traduisent cependant un changement de dimension. À l’horizon se profilent désormais les Jeux de Los Angeles, en 2028. La perspective d’une deuxième médaille olympique sénégalaise est-elle devenue plus concrète ? Les résultats récents de Saly Sarr permettent en tout cas de nourrir cette ambition, sans préjuger du résultat d’une compétition olympique où la concurrence mondiale reste particulièrement relevée. Trente-huit ans après le geste historique de Dia Bâ à Séoul, le Sénégal attend toujours de voir un autre de ses athlètes monter sur un podium olympique. De l’argent décroché en 1988 aux performances récentes de Saly Sarr, l’histoire de l’athlétisme sénégalais s’écrit entre héritage et espoir. À Los Angeles, en 2028, une nouvelle page pourrait s’ouvrir. Par Cheikh Gora DIOP

items.title: Engagement patriotique : La 2ᵉ phase des JEPPC placée sous le signe du « Made in Burkina »
items.description: La deuxième phase de la 3ᵉ édition des Journées nationales d’engagement patriotique et de participation citoyenne (JEPPC) se tiendra du 2 au 16 octobre 2026 au Burkina Faso, sous le thème « Produisons burkinabè, consommons burkinabè ! ». L’annonce a été faite ce vendredi 25 septembre 2026 à Ouagadougou, lors d’une conférence de presse conjointe du Gouvernement. Cette phase vise à promouvoir la production et la consommation locales, soutenir les producteurs et artisans burkinabè, favoriser la création d’emplois et renforcer la souveraineté économique du pays. Le slogan retenu est : « Made in Burkina : faisons de chaque achat un acte de souveraineté ». L’une des principales activités annoncées par le ministre de la Justice Me Edasso Rodrigue Bayala est une exposition gouvernementale des réalisations et acquis de la Révolution progressiste populaire, prévue du 2 au 9 octobre 2026 au Salon international de l’artisanat de Ouagadougou (SIAO). Elle permettra aux visiteurs de découvrir les réalisations des ministères et de bénéficier de divers services administratifs. Plusieurs activités sont également prévues sur l’ensemble du territoire national, notamment des journées de salubrité, des dons de sang, des conférences sur le civisme économique, des foires et des dégustations de mets locaux. Le 15 octobre sera consacré à l’hommage au président Thomas Sankara, tandis que la Nuit des Étoiles du Faso, prévue le 16 octobre, récompensera les meilleurs exemples d’engagement citoyen. Plus de détails à suivre sur Minute.bf
